title: Conceptual and quantitative knowledge of the structure and behavior of matter

sections.body:
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Mass is how much stuff is in an object; volume is how much space it occupies. Density ties them together: it is the amount of mass packed into each unit of volume, and it is the property that tells you whether something floats.

Density is an **intensive** property: it does not depend on how much of the substance you have. A drop of water and a swimming pool of water both have a density of about 1.00 g/cm3. Mass and volume are **extensive** properties: they scale with the amount.

```
D = m / V
D = density (kg/m3, or g/cm3 in lab work)
m = mass (kg; grams in lab work)
V = volume (m3; cm3 or mL in lab work)
1 cm3 = 1 mL exactly
```

**Worked example.** A metal cube has a mass of 54.0 g and each edge is 2.00 cm.

Volume = (2.00 cm)^3 = 8.00 cm3.

D = 54.0 g / 8.00 cm3 = 6.75 g/cm3.

That is denser than water (1.00 g/cm3), so the cube sinks.

To find the volume of an irregular solid, use water displacement: drop it in a graduated cylinder and subtract the starting volume from the final volume.

**Trap:** Heavy objects sink and light objects float. Actually, floating depends on density relative to the fluid, not on weight. A 10,000 kg steel ship floats because its overall density, including the air inside the hull, is less than 1.00 g/cm3, while a 5 g steel bolt sinks.

An atom has a tiny dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by a much larger cloud of electrons. Nearly all the mass is in the nucleus; nearly all the volume is electron cloud.

| Particle | Charge | Mass (approx. amu) | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proton | +1 | 1 | Nucleus |
| Neutron | 0 | 1 | Nucleus |
| Electron | -1 | 1/1836 (about 0.0005) | Orbitals around nucleus |

The **atomic number (Z)** equals the number of protons and defines the element. The **mass number (A)** equals protons plus neutrons.

```
number of neutrons = A - Z
A = mass number (protons + neutrons, unitless count)
Z = atomic number (protons, unitless count)
net charge = protons - electrons (in units of elementary charge)
```

**Worked example.** Carbon-14 is written as 14/6 C. Z = 6, so it has 6 protons. Neutrons = 14 - 6 = 8. Neutral carbon-14 has 6 electrons.

**Worked example 2.** An aluminum ion, Al3+, has Z = 13. Protons = 13. Charge +3 means it lost 3 electrons, so electrons = 13 - 3 = 10.

**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with different neutron counts (same Z, different A). Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 behave identically chemically. The atomic mass printed on the periodic table is a weighted average of the natural isotope mixture, which is why chlorine reads 35.45 rather than a whole number.

**Trap:** Isotopes of an element have different chemical properties. Actually, chemical behavior is set by electron arrangement, which isotopes share. Isotopes differ in mass and in nuclear stability, not in chemistry.

sections.h: The periodic table and periodic trends
sections.body:
The periodic table is arranged by increasing atomic number. **Groups** are the vertical columns and share the same number of valence electrons, which is why they behave alike chemically. **Periods** are the horizontal rows and represent filling the same outer energy level.

| Group | Name | Valence electrons | Signature behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alkali metals | 1 | Very reactive, form +1 ions |
| 2 | Alkaline earth metals | 2 | Reactive, form +2 ions |
| 3 to 12 | Transition metals | varies | Multiple charges, conduct well |
| 17 | Halogens | 7 | Very reactive, form -1 ions |
| 18 | Noble gases | 8 (He has 2) | Full shell, nearly inert |

Key trends, moving **left to right across a period** and **top to bottom down a group**:

| Property | Across a period (left to right) | Down a group |
|---|---|---|
| Atomic radius | Decreases | Increases |
| Ionization energy | Increases | Decreases |
| Electronegativity | Increases | Decreases |
| Metallic character | Decreases | Increases |
| Reactivity of metals | Decreases | Increases |
| Reactivity of nonmetals | Increases | Decreases |

Across a period, protons pile up while electrons stay in the same shell, so the nucleus pulls the cloud in tighter: smaller atoms, harder to remove an electron. Down a group, you add whole new shells, so atoms get bigger and the outer electron is easier to strip.

Metals sit on the left and center: shiny, malleable, ductile, good conductors, and they lose electrons. Nonmetals sit on the upper right: brittle when solid, poor conductors, and they gain electrons. Metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) straddle the staircase and are semiconductors.

**Trap:** Atoms get bigger as you go right across a period because you keep adding particles. Actually radius shrinks going right, because the added protons increase the nuclear pull on the same outer shell.

Atoms bond to reach a stable outer shell, usually eight valence electrons (the octet rule; hydrogen and helium want two). How they get there depends on the electronegativity difference between the partners.

| Bond type | What happens to electrons | Typical partners | Example | Properties |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ionic | Transferred | Metal + nonmetal | NaCl | High melting point, brittle, conducts when dissolved or molten |
| Polar covalent | Shared unequally | Two different nonmetals | H2O, HCl | Dipoles, often soluble in water |
| Nonpolar covalent | Shared equally | Identical or similar nonmetals | O2, CH4 | Low melting point, poor conductor |
| Metallic | Delocalized "sea" of electrons | Metal + metal | Cu, brass | Conducts heat and electricity, malleable, ductile |

In ionic bonding, sodium (1 valence electron) hands its electron to chlorine (7 valence electrons). Sodium becomes Na+, chlorine becomes Cl-, and opposite charges lock into a repeating crystal lattice.

To write an ionic formula, balance the charges to zero. Mg2+ with Cl- needs two chlorides: MgCl2. Al3+ with O2- needs the crisscross: Al2O3.

Water's bent shape plus the polar O-H bonds give the molecule a partially negative oxygen end and partially positive hydrogen ends. Those poles create **hydrogen bonding**, which explains water's high surface tension, high specific heat, high boiling point for its size, and why ice floats.

**Trap:** A covalent bond means the two atoms split the electrons evenly. Actually only bonds between identical or nearly identical atoms are nonpolar. In H2O the oxygen pulls far harder than hydrogen, making a polar bond and a polar molecule, which is the reason water dissolves salts and sugars so well.

sections.h: States of matter and phase changes
sections.body:
The state of a substance is a contest between the kinetic energy of its particles and the attractive forces between them. Solids have fixed shape and fixed volume with particles vibrating in place. Liquids have fixed volume and take the shape of the container. Gases have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume and fill their container. Plasma is ionized gas, found in stars and lightning.

[[diagram:phasechange]]

| Change | From | To | Energy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Melting | Solid | Liquid | Absorbs |
| Freezing | Liquid | Solid | Releases |
| Vaporization (boiling, evaporation) | Liquid | Gas | Absorbs |
| Condensation | Gas | Liquid | Releases |
| Sublimation | Solid | Gas | Absorbs |
| Deposition | Gas | Solid | Releases |

During a phase change the temperature stays constant even though energy keeps flowing in. That energy, called latent heat, goes into breaking intermolecular attractions rather than speeding particles up. On a heating curve this shows as flat plateaus at the melting and boiling points.

```
Q = m * Hf   (melting or freezing)
Q = m * Hv   (boiling or condensing)
Q = energy transferred (J)
m = mass (kg or g)
Hf = latent heat of fusion (J/g); for water, 334 J/g
Hv = latent heat of vaporization (J/g); for water, 2260 J/g
```

**Worked example.** How much energy melts 50.0 g of ice already at 0 degrees C?

Q = (50.0 g)(334 J/g) = 16,700 J, or about 16.7 kJ.

**Trap:** When a pot of water boils, adding more heat makes the water hotter. Actually, once water reaches 100 degrees C at sea level, additional energy converts liquid to steam at constant temperature. Turning the burner higher boils the water away faster; it does not raise the temperature of the liquid.

sections.h: Gas behavior and the gas laws
sections.body:
Gas particles are far apart, move fast and randomly, and collide elastically. Pressure is the result of countless particle collisions with the container walls. Three variables interact: pressure, volume, and Kelvin temperature.

```
Boyle's law:    P1 * V1 = P2 * V2      (temperature constant)
Charles's law:  V1 / T1 = V2 / T2      (pressure constant)
Gay-Lussac:     P1 / T1 = P2 / T2      (volume constant)
Combined:       (P1 * V1) / T1 = (P2 * V2) / T2
P = pressure (Pa; also atm or kPa)
V = volume (m3; also L)
T = absolute temperature (K, kelvin) and it MUST be kelvin
K = degrees C + 273.15
```

**Worked example (Boyle).** A 4.0 L balloon at 1.0 atm is squeezed to 2.0 atm at constant temperature.

V2 = (P1 V1)/P2 = (1.0 atm)(4.0 L)/(2.0 atm) = 2.0 L. Halving the volume doubles the pressure: inverse relationship.

**Worked example (Charles).** A 3.00 L gas sample at 27 degrees C is warmed to 127 degrees C at constant pressure.

T1 = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T2 = 127 + 273 = 400 K.

V2 = V1 * (T2/T1) = 3.00 L * (400/300) = 4.00 L. Direct relationship.

Pressure is also force spread over area:

```
P = F / A
P = pressure (Pa, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m2)
F = force (N)
A = area (m2)
```

**Trap:** You can plug Celsius temperatures into Charles's law as long as you are consistent. Actually, using Celsius gives a wrong answer and can even produce a negative or zero volume. Gas law temperatures must be in kelvin, because kelvin starts at absolute zero where particle motion is minimal.

sections.h: Physical and chemical changes, and conservation of mass
sections.body:
A **physical change** alters form, shape, or state but leaves the substance chemically the same: tearing paper, dissolving salt, melting butter, crushing a can. A **chemical change** rearranges atoms into new substances with new properties: rusting, burning, digesting, cooking an egg, souring milk.

Evidence of a chemical change includes gas bubbles that are not from boiling, an unexpected color change, a precipitate forming in a clear solution, light emitted, and a temperature change the surroundings did not cause.

Distinguish **exothermic** (releases energy, container feels warm, burning and neutralization) from **endothermic** (absorbs energy, container feels cold, photosynthesis and most instant cold packs).

The **law of conservation of mass** says atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products. This is why equations must be balanced: the same count of each atom appears on both sides.

**Worked example.** Balance the combustion of methane.

Unbalanced: CH4 + O2 gives CO2 + H2O.

Balanced: CH4 + 2 O2 gives CO2 + 2 H2O.

Check the atoms. Left: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O. Right: 1 C, 4 H, and 2 + 2 = 4 O. Balanced.

**Worked example 2.** If 4.0 g of methane burns completely with 16.0 g of oxygen and 11.0 g of carbon dioxide forms, how much water forms? Total reactant mass is 20.0 g, so total product mass must be 20.0 g. Water = 20.0 - 11.0 = 9.0 g.

**Trap:** When a log burns down to a small pile of ash, mass was destroyed. Actually, the missing mass left as carbon dioxide and water vapor. Weigh the gases too and the total is unchanged. Only closed-system measurement reveals conservation.

A **pure substance** has one kind of particle: an element (one type of atom, like Cu or O2) or a compound (atoms of different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, like H2O). A **mixture** combines substances physically, in any ratio, with each keeping its own properties, and can be separated physically.

**Homogeneous mixtures (solutions)** look uniform throughout: salt water, air, brass, steel. **Heterogeneous mixtures** have visibly distinct parts: sand in water, salad, granite, oil and vinegar.

Separation techniques map to physical properties: filtration separates by particle size, distillation by boiling point, evaporation removes a volatile solvent, chromatography by how strongly components cling to a medium, and a magnet separates ferromagnetic bits.

In a solution, the **solute** dissolves into the **solvent** (the substance present in greater amount; water is the universal solvent). Concentration can be expressed as:

```
M = n / V
M = molarity (mol/L)
n = moles of solute (mol)
V = volume of solution (L)
```

**Worked example.** Dissolve 0.50 mol of NaCl in enough water to make 2.0 L of solution.

M = 0.50 mol / 2.0 L = 0.25 mol/L, that is 0.25 M.

Dissolving speeds up when you increase temperature, stir, or grind the solute into smaller pieces, all of which increase contact between solute and solvent. Raising temperature increases the solubility of most solids in water but decreases the solubility of gases, which is why a warm soda goes flat and warm river water holds less dissolved oxygen for fish.

**Trap:** Dissolving salt in water is a chemical change because the salt disappears. Actually it is a physical change: the ions disperse but are unchanged, and boiling the water off recovers the original salt.

sections.h: Acids, bases, and the pH scale
sections.body:
Acids donate hydrogen ions (H+) in solution; bases accept H+ or release hydroxide ions (OH-). The pH scale measures the concentration of hydrogen ions.

| pH | Category | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 3 | Strong acid | Stomach acid (about 2), lemon juice (about 2) |
| 4 to 6 | Weak acid | Coffee, tomato juice, normal rain (about 5.6) |
| 7 | Neutral | Pure water |
| 8 to 10 | Weak base | Baking soda solution, seawater (about 8.1) |
| 11 to 14 | Strong base | Ammonia, bleach, lye |

The scale is **logarithmic**: each whole pH unit is a factor of ten in H+ concentration.

```
pH = -log[H+]
[H+] = hydrogen ion concentration (mol/L)
pH is unitless
pH + pOH = 14 (at 25 degrees C)
```

**Worked example.** A solution has [H+] = 1 x 10^-3 mol/L. pH = -log(10^-3) = 3. That is acidic.

**Worked example 2.** How much more acidic is pH 3 than pH 6? The difference is 3 units, so 10^3 = 1000 times more hydrogen ions.

Acid properties: sour taste, turn blue litmus red, react with active metals to release hydrogen gas, react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide. Base properties: bitter taste, slippery feel, turn red litmus blue.

Acid plus base gives **neutralization**, producing a salt and water. Example: HCl + NaOH gives NaCl + H2O.

Indicators to know: litmus (red in acid, blue in base), phenolphthalein (colorless in acid, pink in base), bromothymol blue (yellow in acid, blue in base), and universal indicator or a pH meter for a numeric value.

**Trap:** A pH of 5 is twice as acidic as a pH of 6. Actually it is ten times as acidic, because pH is a base-ten logarithmic scale.

title: Conceptual and quantitative knowledge of forces and motion

sections.h: Describing motion: distance, displacement, speed, velocity
sections.body:
Motion is always described relative to a reference point. **Distance** is total path length traveled, a scalar with magnitude only. **Displacement** is the straight-line change in position from start to finish, a vector with magnitude and direction.

**Speed** is how fast; **velocity** is how fast and in what direction. Average speed uses total distance; average velocity uses displacement.

```
v = d / t
v = speed (m/s)
d = distance (m)
t = time (s)

v_avg = (delta x) / (delta t)
delta x = displacement (m)
delta t = elapsed time (s)
```

**Worked example.** A student walks 40 m east, then 30 m west, in 20 s.

Distance = 40 + 30 = 70 m, so average speed = 70 m / 20 s = 3.5 m/s.

Displacement = 40 m east - 30 m east = 10 m east, so average velocity = 10 m / 20 s = 0.5 m/s east.

On a **position vs. time graph**, the slope is velocity: a straight sloped line is constant velocity, a horizontal line is at rest, and a curve means the velocity is changing. On a **velocity vs. time graph**, the slope is acceleration and the area under the curve is displacement.

**Trap:** Distance and displacement are the same thing measured with different words. Actually they differ any time the path is not a straight line in one direction. A runner who completes one lap of a 400 m track has traveled 400 m of distance but has zero displacement, so her average velocity for the lap is zero even though her average speed was not.

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. Because velocity includes direction, an object accelerates when it speeds up, slows down, or turns, even at constant speed.

```
a = (v_f - v_i) / t
a = acceleration (m/s2)
v_f = final velocity (m/s)
v_i = initial velocity (m/s)
t = time interval (s)

v_f = v_i + a*t
d = v_i*t + (1/2)*a*t^2
v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2*a*d
d = displacement (m)
```

**Worked example.** A car speeds up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5.0 s.

a = (30 - 10) / 5.0 = 20 / 5.0 = 4.0 m/s2.

How far did it travel? d = v_i t + 0.5 a t^2 = (10)(5.0) + 0.5(4.0)(25) = 50 + 50 = 100 m.

**Free fall.** Near Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance, every falling object accelerates downward at g = 9.8 m/s2.

**Worked example.** A ball is dropped from rest and falls for 3.0 s.

v_f = v_i + g t = 0 + (9.8)(3.0) = 29.4 m/s downward.

d = 0.5 g t^2 = 0.5(9.8)(9.0) = 44.1 m.

A negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down. It means the acceleration points in the negative direction. If velocity is also negative, the object is speeding up in that direction.

**Trap:** Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones. Actually, in the absence of air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration, 9.8 m/s2, regardless of mass. A hammer and a feather dropped in a vacuum land together. In air, the feather loses because air resistance is large compared with its weight, not because its mass is small.

**First law (inertia).** An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force. Inertia is resistance to change in motion, and mass is the measure of inertia.

**Second law.** A net force produces acceleration in the direction of that force, proportional to the force and inversely proportional to mass.

```
F_net = m * a
F_net = net force (N, where 1 N = 1 kg*m/s2)
m = mass (kg)
a = acceleration (m/s2)

a = F_net / m
```

**Third law.** For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force, acting on a different object.

**Worked example (second law).** A net force of 12 N acts on a 4.0 kg cart.

a = F/m = 12 N / 4.0 kg = 3.0 m/s2.

**Worked example 2.** A 1200 kg car must accelerate at 2.5 m/s2. Required net force = (1200)(2.5) = 3000 N.

**Net force** is the vector sum. Forces in the same direction add; opposing forces subtract. If a 30 N push right meets 12 N of friction left, F_net = 18 N right. When the net force is zero the object is in **equilibrium**: either at rest or moving at constant velocity, never accelerating.

Third-law pairs never cancel each other, because they act on different objects. A swimmer pushes water backward; the water pushes the swimmer forward. A rocket pushes exhaust gas down; the gas pushes the rocket up. Rockets work in the vacuum of space precisely because they push on their own exhaust, not on air.

**Trap:** A moving object must have a force pushing it forward. Actually, an object moving at constant velocity has zero net force. A puck sliding on frictionless ice keeps going with no forward force at all. Force is needed to change motion, not to maintain it.

**Mass** is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, and it does not change with location. **Weight** is the gravitational force pulling on that mass, measured in newtons, and it changes with the strength of the gravitational field.

```
F_g = m * g
F_g = weight, the force of gravity (N)
m = mass (kg)
g = gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg, or 9.8 m/s2, on Earth)
```

**Worked example.** A student has a mass of 55 kg.

On Earth: weight = (55 kg)(9.8 N/kg) = 539 N.

On the Moon, where g is about 1.6 N/kg: weight = (55)(1.6) = 88 N. Her mass is still 55 kg.

Gravity is a universal attraction between any two masses:

```
F = G * (m1 * m2) / r^2
F = gravitational force (N)
G = universal gravitational constant, 6.67 x 10^-11 N*m2/kg2
m1, m2 = the two masses (kg)
r = distance between their centers (m)
```

The force depends on the product of the masses and the **inverse square** of the distance. Double the separation and the force drops to one fourth. Triple it and the force drops to one ninth.

**Worked example.** Two satellites attract with force F at separation r. If the distance triples, the new force is F / 3^2 = F/9.

Gravity is what keeps planets in orbit and what causes tides. It is always attractive and it never fully disappears; it only gets weaker with distance.

**Trap:** Astronauts float in the space station because there is no gravity in orbit. Actually gravity at that altitude is roughly 90 percent of its surface value. Astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth, moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it. That is apparent weightlessness, not zero gravity.

sections.h: Friction, air resistance, and terminal velocity
sections.body:
Friction is a force that opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact. It arises from microscopic roughness and molecular attraction. It converts kinetic energy into thermal energy, which is why rubbing your hands warms them.

Types to distinguish:

| Type | When it acts | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Static friction | Surfaces at rest relative to each other | Larger than kinetic; must be exceeded to start motion |
| Kinetic (sliding) friction | Surfaces sliding past each other | Roughly constant while sliding |
| Rolling friction | A wheel or ball rolls | Much smaller, which is why wheels help |
| Fluid friction (drag) | Object moves through liquid or gas | Grows rapidly with speed |

```
F_f = mu * F_N
F_f = friction force (N)
mu = coefficient of friction (unitless, depends on the surface pair)
F_N = normal force, perpendicular surface push (N); on level ground F_N = m*g
```

**Worked example.** A 20.0 kg crate sits on a floor with mu = 0.30.

F_N = (20.0 kg)(9.8 m/s2) = 196 N.

F_f = (0.30)(196 N) = 58.8 N. You need to push harder than about 59 N to keep it sliding.

**Terminal velocity.** A falling object speeds up, so drag grows. When upward drag equals downward weight, the net force is zero and the object stops accelerating, falling at constant terminal velocity. A skydiver reaches about 55 m/s in a spread position and roughly 5 m/s under an open parachute, because the chute greatly increases drag area.

**Trap:** Friction is always a nuisance that engineers try to remove. Actually friction is what lets you walk, lets tires grip, and lets brakes stop a car. Without it your shoes would spin uselessly, as they nearly do on ice.

Momentum measures how hard it is to stop a moving object. It depends on both mass and velocity, so a slow truck and a fast bullet can carry comparable momentum.

```
p = m * v
p = momentum (kg*m/s)
m = mass (kg)
v = velocity (m/s), a vector so direction matters

Impulse: J = F * t = delta p
J = impulse (N*s)
F = average force (N)
t = contact time (s)
delta p = change in momentum (kg*m/s)
```

**Worked example.** A 0.145 kg baseball moves at 40.0 m/s.

p = (0.145)(40.0) = 5.80 kg*m/s.

**Worked example 2 (impulse).** A catcher stops that ball in 0.020 s.

F = delta p / t = 5.80 / 0.020 = 290 N.

If she instead lets her glove move back and stretches contact to 0.10 s, F = 5.80 / 0.10 = 58 N. Same momentum change, one fifth the force. That is exactly why airbags, crumple zones, and gymnastic mats work: they extend contact time to reduce peak force.

**Conservation of momentum.** In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after.

```
m1*v1i + m2*v2i = m1*v1f + m2*v2f
```

**Worked example 3.** A 2.0 kg cart at 3.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.0 kg cart and they stick together.

Before: p = (2.0)(3.0) + (1.0)(0) = 6.0 kg*m/s.

After: 6.0 = (3.0 kg)(v), so v = 2.0 m/s in the original direction.

**Trap:** Momentum is just another word for force, or for inertia. Actually momentum is mass times velocity and is a property of a moving object; force is an interaction that changes momentum. A parked truck has huge inertia but zero momentum.

An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. That acceleration points toward the center of the circle, and so does the force causing it.

```
a_c = v^2 / r
a_c = centripetal acceleration (m/s2)
v = tangential speed (m/s)
r = radius of the circular path (m)

F_c = m * v^2 / r
F_c = centripetal force (N), directed toward the center
m = mass (kg)
```

**Worked example.** A 0.20 kg ball swings on a 0.50 m string at 4.0 m/s.

a_c = (4.0)^2 / 0.50 = 16 / 0.50 = 32 m/s2.

F_c = (0.20 kg)(32 m/s2) = 6.4 N, pulling inward along the string.

The centripetal force is always supplied by a real physical agent: string tension for a swinging ball, friction between tires and road for a turning car, gravity for an orbiting moon, the track walls for a roller coaster loop. Cut the string and the ball does not fly outward along the radius; it flies off along a straight tangent line, obeying the first law.

Notice that F_c scales with the square of speed. Doubling the speed of a car in a turn requires four times the friction, which is why speed limits drop sharply on curves. Increasing the radius lowers the required force, which is why highway ramps are built with gentle arcs.

**Trap:** A rider on a spinning ride is thrown outward by centrifugal force. Actually there is no outward force acting on her. She feels pressed against the wall because her body tends to move straight while the wall curves inward and pushes her toward the center. What she calls centrifugal force is inertia interpreted from a rotating frame.

A simple machine does not reduce the work required; it changes the size or direction of the force needed, trading force for distance. The six classic simple machines are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, and screw.

```
MA = F_out / F_in     (actual mechanical advantage)
MA = mechanical advantage (unitless)
F_out = output or resistance force (N)
F_in = input or effort force (N)

IMA (lever) = d_effort / d_resistance   (distances from fulcrum, m)
IMA (inclined plane) = length of ramp / height of ramp (m/m)
Efficiency (%) = (W_out / W_in) * 100
```

**Worked example (lever).** A crowbar has the effort applied 90 cm from the fulcrum and the load 15 cm from the fulcrum.

IMA = 90 / 15 = 6. A 50 N push lifts about 300 N of load, ignoring friction.

**Worked example 2 (ramp).** A 3.0 m ramp rises 0.60 m.

IMA = 3.0 / 0.60 = 5. Lifting a 500 N crate straight up needs 500 N; pushing it up the ideal ramp needs about 100 N, but over five times the distance.

Lever classes: first class has the fulcrum in the middle (seesaw, scissors, crowbar), second class has the load in the middle (wheelbarrow, nutcracker), third class has the effort in the middle (tweezers, a broom, the human forearm). Third-class levers have MA less than one but gain speed and range of motion.

Efficiency is always below 100 percent in a real machine, because friction converts some input work to heat.

**Trap:** A machine with a large mechanical advantage reduces the total work you must do. Actually work output can never exceed work input. A ramp lets you use less force but over a longer distance, so force times distance stays about the same, and friction makes the real total slightly worse.

This is competency 2, skills 7 and 8: types of magnets, characteristics of magnetic fields, and their real-world applications such as solenoids and generators.

Every magnet has a **north-seeking pole** and a **south-seeking pole**. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract, exactly as with electric charge. Poles cannot be separated: cut a bar magnet in half and you get two complete magnets, each with its own north and south. No isolated single pole has ever been found.

A **magnetic field** is the region where a magnet exerts force. We draw it as field lines that leave the north pole, curve around the outside of the magnet to the south pole, and continue from south to north inside the magnet, forming closed loops. Lines never cross, and where they crowd together the field is strongest, which is at the poles. Iron filings or a small compass reveal the pattern.

Only a few materials are strongly magnetic. **Ferromagnetic** metals, iron, nickel, cobalt, and alloys such as steel and alnico, contain **magnetic domains**, tiny regions already magnetized. In an unmagnetized bar the domains point every which way and cancel; stroking it with a magnet or placing it in a strong field lines the domains up. Heating, hammering, or dropping a magnet scrambles the domains again and weakens it.

A **temporary magnet** holds its alignment only while a field is present: a soft iron nail picks up paper clips while touching a magnet and drops them when removed. A **permanent magnet**, made of hardened steel or a neodymium alloy, keeps its domains aligned on its own.

Earth behaves as though a bar magnet were buried in it, tilted about 11 degrees from the rotation axis. The field is generated by convection of the liquid iron outer core, not by a solid magnet. A compass works because its north-seeking pole is attracted toward Earth's northern magnetic pole. Since unlike poles attract, that pole near geographic north is physically a magnetic **south** pole. The offset between magnetic and true north is called declination.

An electric current always creates a magnetic field around it. A straight current-carrying wire is ringed by circular field lines. Wind that wire into a coil, a **solenoid**, and the loops reinforce each other to give a field shaped like a bar magnet's, with a north pole at one end. Slide a soft iron core inside and you have an **electromagnet**, which is far stronger and, crucially, can be switched off. Its strength grows with more current, more turns of wire, and a ferromagnetic core. Scrapyard cranes, doorbells, relays, and speakers all depend on that on-off control.

| Device | Energy conversion | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| Electromagnet | Electrical to magnetic | Current through a coil, iron core concentrates the field |
| Motor | Electrical to mechanical (kinetic) | A current-carrying coil sitting in a magnetic field feels a force and spins |
| Generator | Mechanical (kinetic) to electrical | Turning a coil inside a magnetic field induces a voltage in the coil |

**Electromagnetic induction**, in one sentence: a magnetic field that changes through a coil induces a voltage in that coil, and a current if the circuit is complete. Something must change or move; a magnet sitting still inside a coil induces nothing at all.

**Trap:** Earth's geographic North Pole is a magnetic north pole, since that is where a compass points. Actually the compass needle's own north pole is attracted there, and unlike poles attract, so the magnetic pole near geographic north is a magnetic south pole. The labels on a compass name the direction the needle seeks, not the polarity it meets.

title: Conceptual and quantitative knowledge of energy and its effects

sections.h: Work, power, and the forms of energy
sections.body:
Energy is the capacity to do work. Work is done only when a force moves an object through a distance along the direction of the force.

```
W = F * d
W = work (J, joule, where 1 J = 1 N*m)
F = force applied along the direction of motion (N)
d = displacement (m)

P = W / t   and also   P = F * v
P = power (W, watt, where 1 W = 1 J/s)
W = work or energy transferred (J)
t = time (s)
v = speed (m/s)
```

**Worked example (work).** You push a box with 25 N over 4.0 m.

W = (25 N)(4.0 m) = 100 J.

**Worked example (power).** You lift a 200 N crate 1.5 m in 4.0 s.

W = (200)(1.5) = 300 J. P = 300 J / 4.0 s = 75 W.

If you lift it in 2.0 s instead, the work is the same 300 J but the power doubles to 150 W. Power is about rate, not amount.

Forms of energy to name and recognize: kinetic (motion), gravitational potential (position in a field), elastic potential (stretched or compressed), chemical (bonds, as in food, fuel, batteries), thermal (internal particle motion), electrical, sound, radiant or light, and nuclear (binding energy in the nucleus).

**Trap:** Holding a heavy box motionless is hard, so you must be doing a lot of work on it. Actually, with no displacement, W = F times 0 = 0 J of work on the box. Your muscles burn chemical energy contracting and relaxing, which is why you get tired, but physics work on the box is zero. Likewise carrying a suitcase horizontally does no work against gravity, because the force is vertical and the motion is horizontal.

sections.h: Kinetic and potential energy, and conservation
sections.body:
Kinetic energy is energy of motion. Gravitational potential energy is stored energy of height. In a system with no friction, energy converts between the two while the total stays constant.

```
KE = (1/2) * m * v^2
KE = kinetic energy (J)
m = mass (kg)
v = speed (m/s)

PE = m * g * h
PE = gravitational potential energy (J)
g = 9.8 m/s2
h = height above the reference point (m)

Mechanical energy: KE + PE = constant (no friction)
```

**Worked example (KE).** A 1000 kg car travels at 20 m/s.

KE = 0.5(1000)(20)^2 = 0.5(1000)(400) = 200,000 J = 200 kJ.

Now double the speed to 40 m/s: KE = 0.5(1000)(1600) = 800 kJ. Four times the energy, which is why stopping distance grows so sharply with speed.

**Worked example (PE and conversion).** A 2.0 kg ball is held 5.0 m above the ground.

PE = (2.0)(9.8)(5.0) = 98 J.

Dropped, at the instant before impact all of it is kinetic: 98 J = 0.5(2.0)v^2, so v^2 = 98, and v = 9.9 m/s.

A pendulum shows the trade cleanly: PE is maximum and KE is zero at the top of each swing; KE is maximum and PE is minimum at the bottom. In the real world a pendulum eventually stops because friction and air drag convert mechanical energy to thermal energy, which is still conserved overall.

**Trap:** Doubling the speed of a car doubles its kinetic energy. Actually kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples KE. Momentum doubles; energy quadruples. This is the single most common quantitative error on energy items.

**Temperature** is the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample. **Thermal energy** is the total kinetic energy of all the particles, so it depends on how much material there is. **Heat** is thermal energy in transit, and it always flows spontaneously from hotter to colder until thermal equilibrium.

```
Q = m * c * (delta T)
Q = heat transferred (J)
m = mass (kg or g, matching c)
c = specific heat capacity (J/(g*degC)); water = 4.18 J/(g*degC)
delta T = change in temperature (degrees C or K; the size of a degree is the same)

K = degrees C + 273.15
degrees F = (9/5)*degrees C + 32
```

**Worked example.** How much heat raises 200 g of water from 20.0 to 50.0 degrees C?

delta T = 30.0 degrees C.

Q = (200 g)(4.18 J/(g*degC))(30.0 degC) = 25,080 J, about 25.1 kJ.

**Worked example 2.** Convert 25 degrees C to Fahrenheit: (9/5)(25) + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77 degrees F. And to kelvin: 25 + 273 = 298 K.

Water's specific heat is unusually high, so it absorbs a lot of energy per degree. That is why coastal areas have milder temperature swings than inland areas, why a lake stays cool on a hot afternoon while the sand burns your feet, and why water is the working fluid in car radiators.

**Absolute zero** is 0 K, or -273.15 degrees C, the point of minimum particle motion. Negative kelvin temperatures do not exist.

**Trap:** A large iceberg is colder than a cup of ice water because it contains far more cold. Actually both can sit at the same temperature, 0 degrees C. The iceberg has vastly more thermal energy in total because it has vastly more mass. Temperature is an average per particle; thermal energy is a total.

Thermal energy moves in exactly three ways, and test items usually turn on identifying which one dominates in a described scenario.

| Mode | Mechanism | Needs matter? | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conduction | Direct particle-to-particle collisions in contact | Yes, best in solids | Metal spoon heats up in hot soup |
| Convection | Bulk movement of heated fluid, driven by density differences | Yes, fluids only | Boiling water circulating; sea breeze; mantle cells |
| Radiation | Electromagnetic waves | No, works in vacuum | Sunlight warming your face; heat felt near a fire |

**Conduction** works best in metals, whose free electrons carry energy quickly. Insulators such as wood, plastic, fiberglass, and still air conduct poorly because they lack mobile charge carriers and often trap air pockets.

**Convection currents** form because warm fluid expands, becomes less dense, and rises while cooler dense fluid sinks to replace it. This single pattern explains hot air rising to a ceiling, thunderstorm updrafts, ocean circulation, and mantle convection that drives plate motion.

**Radiation** requires no medium, which is how the Sun's energy crosses 150 million km of near vacuum. Dark, matte surfaces absorb and emit radiation well; shiny, light surfaces reflect it. That is why a thermos uses a silvered vacuum wall: the vacuum blocks conduction and convection, and the mirror finish blocks radiation.

**Worked application.** A pot of water on a gas burner uses all three: radiation from the flame, conduction through the metal pot bottom, and convection inside the water.

**Trap:** Cold flows into a warm object to cool it down. Actually cold is not a substance and does not flow. Only thermal energy transfers, and always from warmer to cooler. An ice cube does not push cold into your drink; the drink loses heat to the ice.

sections.h: The laws of thermodynamics and energy conservation
sections.body:
The **first law of thermodynamics** is conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed or transferred. Track energy through any device and the totals balance.

```
Efficiency (%) = (useful energy output / total energy input) * 100
```

**Worked example.** A motor draws 500 J of electrical energy and delivers 350 J of mechanical work.

Efficiency = (350 / 500) * 100 = 70 percent. The other 150 J left as thermal energy and sound.

The **second law** says that in every real energy transformation some energy disperses as low-grade thermal energy, so entropy (disorder) in the universe increases. No real machine is 100 percent efficient, and heat will not flow spontaneously from a cold body to a hot one. A refrigerator does move heat from cold to hot, but only by consuming electrical energy, and it dumps more heat into the kitchen than it removes from the food.

Energy transformation chains are useful to trace. A flashlight: chemical in battery, to electrical in the circuit, to radiant and thermal at the bulb. A hydroelectric dam: gravitational potential, to kinetic in the falling water, to mechanical rotation in the turbine, to electrical in the generator. Photosynthesis: radiant to chemical.

Distinguish **renewable** sources (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass, tidal) from **nonrenewable** (coal, oil, natural gas, uranium). Nuclear fission splits heavy nuclei and powers reactors; nuclear fusion joins light nuclei and powers stars, releasing far more energy per unit mass.

**Trap:** A device could be built that runs forever with no energy input, if we just reduce friction enough. Actually the second law forbids it. Even with tiny friction, every transformation leaks some energy as heat, so a perpetual motion machine is impossible, not merely unbuilt.

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy without transferring matter. **Transverse** waves vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel (light, waves on a rope, S waves). **Longitudinal** or compressional waves vibrate parallel to travel (sound, P waves). **Mechanical** waves need a medium; **electromagnetic** waves do not.

[[diagram:wave]]

Parts of a wave: crest, trough, amplitude (maximum displacement from rest, which sets loudness or brightness), wavelength (crest to crest), frequency (cycles per second), and period.

```
v = f * lambda
v = wave speed (m/s)
f = frequency (Hz, where 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second)
lambda = wavelength (m)

T = 1 / f
T = period (s)
```

**Worked example.** A wave has frequency 5.0 Hz and wavelength 2.0 m.

v = (5.0)(2.0) = 10 m/s. Its period is T = 1/5.0 = 0.20 s.

**Worked example 2.** Sound travels about 343 m/s in air at 20 degrees C. A 686 Hz tone has lambda = v/f = 343/686 = 0.50 m.

Wave behaviors: **reflection** (bounces off a boundary, angle in equals angle out), **refraction** (bends when speed changes on entering a new medium), **diffraction** (spreads around edges and through openings), **interference** (constructive when crests align, destructive when a crest meets a trough), and **standing waves** with nodes and antinodes.

The **Doppler effect** raises observed frequency as a source approaches and lowers it as the source recedes, which is why a siren drops in pitch as it passes and why redshift reveals galaxies moving away.

**Trap:** A wave carries the water, air, or rope along with it. Actually the medium's particles oscillate about a fixed position and return. A duck bobbing on a lake goes up and down, not toward shore. Only energy propagates.

sections.h: The electromagnetic spectrum, light, and sound
sections.body:
Electromagnetic waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel through vacuum at the speed of light, c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s. They differ only in wavelength and frequency, which vary inversely.

[[diagram:emspectrum]]

```
c = f * lambda
c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s (speed of light in vacuum)
f = frequency (Hz)
lambda = wavelength (m)
```

In order of increasing frequency and energy, decreasing wavelength:

| Band | Relative wavelength | Typical use or effect |
|---|---|---|
| Radio | Longest | Broadcast, MRI, radio astronomy |
| Microwave | Long | Cooking, radar, cell and Wi-Fi |
| Infrared | Longer than red | Thermal imaging, remote controls |
| Visible | 400 to 700 nm | Human sight, photosynthesis |
| Ultraviolet | Shorter than violet | Sunburn, vitamin D, sterilization |
| X-ray | Very short | Medical imaging of bone |
| Gamma | Shortest | Nuclear decay, cancer therapy |

Mnemonic for the order: **R**adio **M**icrowave **I**nfrared **V**isible **U**ltraviolet **X**-ray **G**amma, remembered as "Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns."

Within visible light, ROYGBIV runs from longest wavelength (red) to shortest (violet), so violet carries the most energy per photon.

**Worked example.** Green light with lambda = 5.0 x 10^-7 m has f = c/lambda = (3.00 x 10^8)/(5.0 x 10^-7) = 6.0 x 10^14 Hz.

Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave. It travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases, and not at all in a vacuum. Pitch corresponds to frequency; loudness corresponds to amplitude and is measured in decibels. Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

**Trap:** In space, an explosion would produce a loud boom. Actually sound requires a material medium to compress, and space is nearly empty, so no sound reaches you. Light from the explosion does arrive, because electromagnetic waves need no medium.

Like charges repel, unlike charges attract, and charge is never created or destroyed, only moved. In everyday matter it is electrons that move. An object charges by **friction** (rubbing transfers electrons, leaving one material negative and the other positive), by **conduction** (a charged object touches a neutral one and they share charge, so both end up with the same sign), or by **induction** (a charged object brought near, without touching, separates the charge inside a neutral object, which is why a charged comb picks up neutral paper).

[[diagram:circuits]]

**Conductors** such as copper and salt water have loosely held electrons that move freely. **Insulators** such as rubber, glass, and dry air hold electrons tightly. **Semiconductors** such as silicon conduct only under certain conditions, which is what makes chips and solar cells possible.

**Current** is the rate charge flows past a point. **Voltage** is the energy delivered per unit of charge, so it is the push. **Resistance** opposes flow and turns electrical energy into heat and light; it rises with a longer wire, a thinner wire, and a higher temperature.

```
I = q / t
I = current (A, ampere, where 1 A = 1 C/s)
q = charge passing a point (C, coulomb)
t = time (s)

V = I * R          (Ohm's law)
V = voltage, potential difference (V, volt, where 1 V = 1 J/C)
R = resistance (ohm)

P = I * V = I^2 * R
P = electrical power (W, watt = J/s)
E = P * t = electrical energy used (J; utilities bill it in kWh)
```

**Worked example (Ohm's law).** A 12 V battery drives current through a 4.0 ohm resistor. I = V/R = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A. Double the resistance to 8.0 ohm at the same voltage and I = 1.5 A: at fixed voltage, current and resistance are inversely related.

**Worked example (power).** A hair dryer draws 10.0 A from a 120 V outlet. P = IV = (10.0)(120) = 1200 W. Check it the other way: R = V/I = 12 ohm, so P = I^2 R = (100)(12) = 1200 W. Running it 15 minutes uses (1.2 kW)(0.25 h) = 0.30 kWh.

| Feature | Series | Parallel |
|---|---|---|
| Current path | One single loop | Two or more branches |
| Total resistance | Sum of the parts, larger than any one part | Less than the smallest single resistance |
| Current | The same at every point in the loop | Divides among branches, most through the least resistance |
| Voltage | Divides among components, and the parts add to the source voltage | Full source voltage across every branch |
| One bulb removed | Loop broken, everything goes out | Others stay lit at the same brightness |

An **ammeter** is wired **in series** so the current it reads passes through it, and it has very low resistance. A **voltmeter** is wired **in parallel**, across the two ends of a component, and it has very high resistance so it draws almost no current.

The water analogy keeps this straight: voltage is pump pressure, current is flow rate, resistance is a narrow pipe. A battery with an open switch is a pump behind a closed valve, full pressure and no flow, which is why voltage can exist with no current.

**Trap:** Current is used up as it goes around a circuit, so the last bulb in a series string is dimmest. Actually charge is conserved, so exactly as much current leaves a bulb as enters it, and identical series bulbs glow equally. What gets used up is energy, not charge, and voltage is the quantity that drops across each component.

sections.h: Light and optics: reflection, refraction, and lenses
sections.body:
Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium, which is why ray diagrams work. At a boundary, two rules govern everything.

**Reflection.** The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, with both angles measured from the **normal**, the line perpendicular to the surface, not from the surface itself.

**Regular (specular) reflection** happens on a smooth surface: parallel rays stay parallel after bouncing, so you get a clear image in a mirror or still water. **Diffuse reflection** happens on a rough surface: each tiny facet still obeys the law, but the facets point different ways, so the rays scatter and no image forms. Diffuse reflection is how you see this page: the law is never violated, only the surface differs.

**Refraction.** Light changes speed entering a new medium, and if it arrives at an angle that speed change bends it. A slower medium bends the ray toward the normal, a faster medium bends it away. The **index of refraction** measures how much a medium slows light, so a higher index means slower light and more bending.

```
n = c / v
n = index of refraction (unitless)
c = speed of light in vacuum, 3.00 x 10^8 m/s
v = speed of light in that medium (m/s)
n = 1.00 for vacuum, about 1.33 for water, about 1.5 for common glass

Total magnification of a compound microscope = (objective power) x (eyepiece power)
```

**Worked example.** Light moves at 2.0 x 10^8 m/s inside a plastic block. n = (3.00 x 10^8)/(2.0 x 10^8) = 1.5. That beats water's 1.33, so light bends more entering this plastic than entering water.

When light tries to leave a slower medium for a faster one at a shallow enough angle it does not escape: past the **critical angle** it reflects entirely back inside. That is **total internal reflection**, which keeps a signal bouncing down an optical fiber for kilometers with little loss.

| Feature | Convex (converging) lens | Concave (diverging) lens |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | Thicker at the middle | Thinner at the middle |
| Effect on parallel rays | Bends them together to a focal point | Spreads them apart |
| Object beyond the focal point | Real, inverted image you can project on a screen | No real image, ever |
| Object inside the focal length | Virtual, upright, enlarged (magnifying glass) | Virtual, upright, reduced |
| Typical uses | Camera, projector, eyepiece, farsighted correction | Nearsighted correction, peepholes |

In the eye, the cornea does most of the bending and the flexible **lens** fine-tunes focus by changing shape, called accommodation. The image on the retina is real and inverted, and the brain interprets it right side up. A nearsighted eye focuses in front of the retina, so it is corrected with a **concave** lens that spreads the light first. A farsighted eye would focus behind the retina, so it takes a **convex** lens.

Instruments stack lenses. A refracting telescope uses a large objective lens to gather light from a distant object and form a real image that the eyepiece magnifies. A compound microscope does the same with a short-focal-length objective close to the specimen. **Worked example 2.** A 40x objective with a 10x eyepiece gives 40 x 10 = 400x total magnification.

**Dispersion** occurs because the index of refraction varies slightly with wavelength. Violet slows and bends most, red least, so a prism fans white light into the spectrum and raindrops make a rainbow.

**Trap:** Light always bends when it passes into a different material. Actually a ray that strikes the boundary head on, traveling straight along the normal, changes speed and wavelength but keeps going in a straight line. Bending requires striking at an angle, so one edge of the wavefront slows before the other. Note also that frequency never changes in refraction; wavelength does.

title: Knowledge of Earth and the processes that affect it

sections.body:
Earth is layered by both composition and physical behavior, and the two systems of names are often confused.

[[diagram:earthlayers]]

By **composition**, from outside in: crust (silicate rock, thin), mantle (denser iron and magnesium silicates, by far the largest volume), core (iron and nickel).

By **physical state**: lithosphere (rigid crust plus uppermost mantle, broken into plates), asthenosphere (weak, slowly flowing upper mantle that plates ride on), mesosphere or lower mantle (stiffer solid), outer core (liquid), inner core (solid).

| Layer | Composition | State | Approximate thickness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continental crust | Granitic, less dense | Solid | 30 to 50 km |
| Oceanic crust | Basaltic, denser | Solid | 5 to 10 km |
| Mantle | Fe and Mg silicates | Solid but plastic flow | About 2900 km |
| Outer core | Iron, nickel | Liquid | About 2200 km |
| Inner core | Iron, nickel | Solid | Radius about 1200 km |

Temperature and pressure both increase with depth. The inner core is hotter than the outer core yet stays solid because the immense pressure prevents melting.

The circulation of the liquid outer core generates Earth's **magnetic field** by the dynamo effect. That field deflects charged solar wind particles, protects the atmosphere, produces auroras near the poles, and is why a compass needle aligns north. Magnetic reversals recorded in seafloor basalt provided key evidence for seafloor spreading.

Seismic waves reveal all of this: P waves (primary, longitudinal, fastest, travel through solids and liquids) and S waves (secondary, transverse, slower, blocked by liquids). The S wave shadow zone is how we know the outer core is liquid.

**Trap:** The tectonic plates float on a sea of liquid magma. Actually the asthenosphere is solid rock that deforms plastically over long timescales, like very stiff putty. Magma exists only in localized pockets, not as a global liquid layer.

The lithosphere is broken into plates that move a few centimeters per year, driven by mantle convection, ridge push, and slab pull. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift based on matching coastlines, identical fossils on separated continents, matching rock and mountain belts, and glacial deposits in now-tropical regions. He lacked a mechanism; mid-twentieth-century mapping of mid-ocean ridges, seafloor age, and magnetic stripes supplied it.

[[diagram:boundaries]]

| Boundary | Relative motion | Crust result | Features | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Divergent | Plates move apart | New crust created | Mid-ocean ridge, rift valley, shallow quakes, basaltic volcanism | Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift |
| Convergent, ocean to continent | Collide, denser ocean plate subducts | Crust destroyed | Deep trench, volcanic arc, strong deep quakes | Andes, Cascades |
| Convergent, ocean to ocean | Collide, older plate subducts | Crust destroyed | Trench, island arc | Japan, Aleutians |
| Convergent, continent to continent | Collide, neither subducts | Crust thickened | Folded mountains, no volcanism | Himalayas, Appalachians |
| Transform | Slide past horizontally | Neither created nor destroyed | Strike-slip faults, shallow quakes, no volcanoes | San Andreas Fault |

Earthquake magnitude is measured on a logarithmic moment magnitude scale: each whole step is roughly 32 times more released energy and about 10 times greater ground amplitude. The **focus** is the underground point of rupture; the **epicenter** is the point on the surface directly above it. Locating an epicenter requires seismograms from three stations, using the P wave to S wave arrival gap to find distance, then triangulating.

Pangaea assembled roughly 300 million years ago and began breaking up about 200 million years ago.

**Trap:** Earthquakes happen only at convergent boundaries. Actually all three boundary types produce earthquakes. Divergent and transform boundaries produce shallow quakes; only subduction zones produce very deep ones.

sections.h: Rocks, minerals, and the rock cycle
sections.body:
A **mineral** is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered crystal structure. A **rock** is a solid aggregate of one or more minerals. Coal and pearl are not minerals, because they are organic in origin.

[[diagram:rockcycle]]

Mineral identification properties: hardness (Mohs scale 1 talc to 10 diamond), color (least reliable), streak (color of powder, more reliable), luster (metallic or nonmetallic), cleavage or fracture, density, crystal form, and special tests such as reaction with acid or magnetism.

| Rock type | How it forms | Key textures | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Igneous, intrusive | Magma cools slowly underground | Coarse, visible crystals | Granite, diorite |
| Igneous, extrusive | Lava cools quickly at surface | Fine grained or glassy, may be vesicular | Basalt, obsidian, pumice |
| Sedimentary, clastic | Compaction and cementation of sediment | Layered, often with fossils | Sandstone, shale, conglomerate |
| Sedimentary, chemical or organic | Precipitation or accumulated remains | Crystalline or fossiliferous | Limestone, rock salt, coal |
| Metamorphic, foliated | Heat and pressure align minerals | Banded, layered | Slate, schist, gneiss |
| Metamorphic, nonfoliated | Heat and pressure, uniform minerals | No banding | Marble (from limestone), quartzite (from sandstone) |

The rock cycle has no fixed starting point and no required sequence. Igneous rock can weather to sediment, or metamorphose directly. Sedimentary rock can melt or metamorphose. Any rock that melts and re-solidifies becomes igneous.

Key processes: weathering breaks rock down, erosion transports it, deposition drops it, compaction and cementation lithify it, heat and pressure metamorphose it, melting and cooling make igneous rock.

**Trap:** Metamorphic rock forms when rock melts and recrystallizes. Actually metamorphism happens in the solid state. Once rock fully melts it becomes magma, and cooling that magma yields igneous rock, not metamorphic rock.

**Weathering** breaks rock apart in place. **Erosion** carries the pieces away. Confusing the two is a frequent error.

**Mechanical (physical) weathering** breaks rock without changing its chemistry: frost wedging (water expands about 9 percent on freezing in cracks), abrasion by wind and water, root wedging, exfoliation from pressure release, and salt crystal growth.

**Chemical weathering** changes rock composition: carbonation (carbonic acid from dissolved CO2 dissolves limestone), oxidation (iron plus oxygen makes rust-colored iron oxide), hydrolysis (water reacts with feldspar to form clay), and acid from lichens or acid rain. Chemical weathering runs fastest where it is hot and wet, which is why Florida and the tropics weather chemically far faster than a cold dry desert.

Surface area controls rate. Break one large block into many small ones and total exposed surface climbs sharply, so weathering accelerates.

Soil forms from weathered parent rock plus organic matter, and develops horizons:

| Horizon | Common name | Content |
|---|---|---|
| O | Litter | Fresh and decaying organic matter |
| A | Topsoil | Humus mixed with minerals, most fertile |
| E | Eluviation | Leached, light colored |
| B | Subsoil | Accumulated clay, iron, minerals washed down |
| C | Parent material | Partly weathered rock fragments |
| R | Bedrock | Unweathered rock |

Agents of erosion and their signature landforms: running water (V-shaped valleys, meanders, deltas, floodplains, alluvial fans), glaciers (U-shaped valleys, moraines, cirques, erratics), wind (dunes, deflation hollows, desert pavement), waves (sea cliffs, sea arches, barrier islands, spits), and gravity (landslides, slump, creep).

**Trap:** Weathering and erosion mean the same thing. Actually weathering is breakdown in place while erosion is transport. A crumbling gravestone is weathering; the silt in a river is erosion at work.

sections.h: Florida geology: carbonate platform, karst, and aquifer
sections.body:
Florida's geology is unusual and is fair game on this exam, so learn it as its own unit.

**Carbonate platform.** The Florida Peninsula sits atop the Florida Platform, a broad limestone and dolostone plateau far wider than the visible land, extending west beneath the Gulf and east toward the Atlantic shelf. The platform accumulated over tens of millions of years as shallow warm marine water deposited calcium carbonate from shells, coral, and algae. That means Florida's bedrock is chemical and biological **sedimentary rock**, essentially compressed ancient seafloor.

**No native surface igneous rock.** Florida has no volcanoes, no exposed granite, and no surface igneous or metamorphic bedrock. Any granite countertop or basalt landscaping stone in Florida was imported. Igneous basement rock exists only thousands of feet down, buried under the carbonate sequence.

**Karst topography.** Limestone dissolves in weak carbonic acid, formed when rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from air and soil. Over time this creates a karst landscape: caves, underground channels, disappearing streams, springs, and sinkholes. Florida has more first-magnitude springs than any comparable region, including Silver Springs and Wakulla Springs.

**Sinkholes** form when a limestone void grows until the overlying sand and clay collapse into it. Drought, heavy rain after drought, and heavy groundwater pumping all raise sinkhole risk, because the water in a cavity helps support the roof. The corridor from roughly Tampa through Ocala and Gainesville is the highest-risk zone.

**Floridan aquifer system.** This is one of the most productive aquifers in the world, held in porous limestone, and it supplies most of Florida's drinking water. It is confined by clay in some areas and unconfined and highly vulnerable in others. Because water moves quickly through karst conduits with little filtration, surface pollutants like fertilizer nitrate, septic effluent, and spills can reach drinking water fast.

**Phosphate deposits.** Central Florida's Bone Valley, in the Polk and Hillsborough county area, holds marine phosphate rock rich in the fossilized remains of marine organisms. It is mined for fertilizer and is a large part of the state economy. Mining creates gypsum stacks and reclamation obligations, and phosphogypsum contains low-level radioactivity.

**Sandy soils.** Much of Florida is covered by quartz sand reworked by ancient shorelines and wind, producing soils that drain very fast, hold few nutrients, and are often acidic in scrub. Coastal ridges are relict dune and beach lines from higher sea levels.

**Sea level change.** During Pleistocene glacial maxima, sea level dropped over 100 m and Florida was more than twice its present width. During interglacial highs, most of the peninsula was submerged, which is why marine fossils appear well inland. Present sea level rise makes low-lying South Florida especially vulnerable, and because the bedrock is porous limestone, seawalls cannot stop water from moving up through the rock.

**Trap:** Florida's sinkholes are caused by underground rivers eroding tunnels the way a surface stream cuts a canyon. Actually the dominant process is chemical dissolution of limestone by acidic groundwater, not mechanical scouring. The collapse is the final surface symptom of long, slow dissolution.

Dry air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen by volume, with the remaining 1 percent argon plus trace gases including carbon dioxide (roughly 0.04 percent). Water vapor varies from near zero to about 4 percent and is not counted in the dry-air figures.

[[diagram:atmosphere]]

Layers from the ground up, with the boundary each time named for the layer below (tropopause, stratopause, mesopause):

| Layer | Altitude range (approx.) | Temperature trend with height | Key features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troposphere | 0 to 12 km | Decreases | Nearly all weather and water vapor, most of the mass |
| Stratosphere | 12 to 50 km | Increases | Ozone layer absorbs UV; jets cruise here; stable |
| Mesosphere | 50 to 80 km | Decreases | Coldest layer; meteors burn up here |
| Thermosphere | 80 to 600 km | Increases | Auroras; ISS orbits here; ionosphere reflects radio |
| Exosphere | Above 600 km | Effectively none | Fades into space |

Mnemonic for order: **T**he **S**ky **M**ust **T**ouch **E**verything.

Temperature in the stratosphere rises with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation there and converts it to heat. This inversion makes the layer very stable, which is why storms top out at the tropopause and spread into anvil shapes.

Air pressure always decreases with altitude, because less atmosphere sits above you. About half the atmosphere's mass lies below 5.5 km. Standard sea level pressure is 101.3 kPa, 1013 mb, or 1 atm.

Distinguish the two ozone stories: stratospheric ozone is beneficial and was thinned by CFCs, addressed by the Montreal Protocol. Ground-level ozone is a harmful pollutant formed by sunlight acting on vehicle exhaust.

**Trap:** The atmosphere gets steadily colder the higher you go. Actually temperature alternates direction four times, which is exactly how the layers are defined. It falls in the troposphere, rises in the stratosphere, falls in the mesosphere, and rises in the thermosphere.

**Weather** is atmospheric conditions right now in one place. **Climate** is the long-term pattern of weather for a region, conventionally averaged over 30 years.

Uneven solar heating drives everything. The equator receives sunlight at a high angle year round and the poles at a low angle spread over more area, creating pressure differences and therefore wind. Air moves from high pressure toward low pressure. The **Coriolis effect** deflects moving air right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern, producing the trade winds, prevailing westerlies, and polar easterlies rather than straight north-south flow.

| Front | Motion | Weather |
|---|---|---|
| Cold front | Cold air pushes under warm | Brief intense storms, then cooler and drier; steep clouds |
| Warm front | Warm air rides over cold | Long steady light precipitation, then warmer and humid |
| Stationary front | Neither advances | Prolonged clouds and rain |
| Occluded front | Cold front overtakes warm | Complex, widespread precipitation |

Low pressure means rising air, cooling, condensation, clouds, and storms. High pressure means sinking air, warming, and clear skies. In the Northern Hemisphere, air spirals counterclockwise and inward around a low, clockwise and outward around a high.

Relative humidity is the ratio of water vapor present to the maximum the air can hold at that temperature. Cooling air to its **dew point** produces condensation: dew, fog, or cloud.

Cloud names combine altitude and form: cirrus is high and wispy ice, stratus is low and layered with drizzle, cumulus is puffy fair-weather, and cumulonimbus is the tall thunderstorm cloud. The prefix nimbo or suffix nimbus signals precipitation.

**Trap:** Clouds form because warm air holds more water and then the water gets heavy and falls. Actually clouds form when rising air expands and cools to the dew point, so vapor condenses on tiny particles. Rising and cooling is the trigger, not weight.

sections.h: The water cycle and Earth's water budget
sections.body:
Water cycles endlessly among ocean, atmosphere, land, and living things, powered by solar energy and gravity. It is a closed system on the scale of the planet: the total amount is essentially constant.

Processes to name precisely: **evaporation** (liquid to vapor from water bodies), **transpiration** (vapor released through plant stomata), **evapotranspiration** (the combined term), **sublimation** (ice directly to vapor), **condensation** (vapor to droplets, forming clouds), **precipitation** (rain, snow, sleet, hail), **infiltration** (water soaking into soil), **percolation** (downward movement to groundwater), **runoff** (surface flow to streams), and **groundwater flow** (slow movement through aquifers to springs and the sea).

Distribution of Earth's water, which is worth memorizing as approximate figures:

| Reservoir | Share of all water |
|---|---|
| Oceans (saline) | About 97 percent |
| Glaciers and ice caps | About 2 percent |
| Groundwater | Under 1 percent |
| Lakes, rivers, soil, atmosphere, biosphere | Small fraction of 1 percent |

So fresh liquid surface water, the kind people most directly use, is a tiny slice of the total, and most fresh water is locked in ice.

Key vocabulary: a **watershed** is all the land draining to a common outlet. The **water table** is the top of the saturated zone. An **aquifer** is a permeable rock body that stores and transmits water. **Permeability** is how easily water flows through, **porosity** is how much void space exists. Gravel is both porous and permeable; clay is porous but nearly impermeable, so it makes a confining layer.

Paving over land reduces infiltration and increases runoff, which raises flood risk and reduces aquifer recharge.

**Trap:** Water evaporating from the ocean loses only some of its salt, so rain is slightly salty. Actually evaporation leaves essentially all dissolved salt behind, which is why precipitation is fresh and why the ocean stays saline.

sections.h: Geologic time, fossils, and dating methods
sections.body:
Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Life appears in the record by roughly 3.5 billion years ago as prokaryotes, oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere by about 2.4 billion years ago through cyanobacterial photosynthesis, and complex multicellular animals diversified in the Cambrian about 540 million years ago.

**Relative dating** puts events in order without giving numeric ages, using a small set of principles:

| Principle | Statement |
|---|---|
| Superposition | In undisturbed layers, lower is older |
| Original horizontality | Sediment settles in flat layers, so tilted layers were deformed later |
| Cross-cutting relationships | A fault or intrusion is younger than the rock it cuts |
| Inclusions | Fragments inside a rock are older than the rock containing them |
| Faunal succession | Fossil assemblages appear in a consistent, recognizable order |

An **unconformity** is a gap in the record where erosion removed layers or no deposition occurred.

**Absolute dating** uses radioactive decay to give numeric ages.

```
After n half-lives, remaining fraction = (1/2)^n
n = number of half-lives elapsed (unitless)
Age = n * (half-life)
```

**Worked example.** A sample contains one eighth of its original carbon-14. Since (1/2)^3 = 1/8, three half-lives have passed. Carbon-14's half-life is 5730 years, so age = 3 x 5730 = 17,190 years.

Match the method to the material: carbon-14 dates once-living material up to roughly 50,000 years; potassium-argon and uranium-lead date igneous and metamorphic rocks over millions to billions of years.

**Index fossils** are species that were widespread but existed for only a short interval, making them excellent time markers. Trilobites mark the Paleozoic; ammonites help mark the Mesozoic.

**Trap:** Carbon-14 dating is used to determine the age of dinosaur fossils and of rocks. Actually carbon-14 is useless past about 50,000 years and applies only to formerly living carbon-bearing material. Dinosaur ages come from radiometric dating of the surrounding igneous or volcanic layers.

sections.h: Reading maps and charts: topographic, geologic, and weather
sections.body:
**Topographic maps** show the shape of the land with **contour lines**, each connecting points of equal elevation. The **contour interval** is the vertical distance between neighboring lines; it is constant across a map and stated in the legend. **Index contours** are the heavier, labeled lines, normally every fifth one.

The rules that generate most test items: contour lines never cross, since one spot cannot have two elevations. Spacing shows steepness, so lines close together mean a steep slope and lines far apart a gentle one. Closed loops are a hill, with the innermost loop as the summit. Loops drawn with short **hachure** ticks pointing inward mark a depression, and the first hachured line has the same elevation as the ordinary contour just outside it. Where contours cross a stream they bend into a **V that points upstream**.

**Worked example.** Index contours read 200 ft and 250 ft with four unlabeled lines between them. That is five equal steps across 50 ft, so the contour interval is 10 ft.

**Worked example 2 (gradient).** Point A is at 300 ft, point B at 100 ft, 4 mi apart. Gradient = 200 ft / 4 mi = 50 ft per mile.

To draw a **topographic profile**, lay a paper strip along the line of interest, tick where each contour meets it, transfer the ticks to a graph with distance across and elevation up, and connect the points smoothly. Profiles usually exaggerate the vertical scale, which makes real slopes look steeper than they are.

**Geologic maps** use color and pattern for the rock unit exposed at the surface, plus symbols for faults, contacts, and the tilt of beds. A **cross section** is a vertical slice showing those units at depth. Read one with the relative dating principles: by **superposition**, in undisturbed layers the lowest bed is oldest and the top is youngest; by **cross-cutting relationships**, a fault, dike, or intrusion is younger than everything it cuts; and folding or tilting came after the beds it deformed.

**Weather maps** use **isobars**, lines of equal pressure in millibars, and **isotherms**, lines of equal temperature. Tightly packed isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and strong wind. H marks a high, with sinking air and fair skies; L marks a low, with rising air, clouds, and storms. A **station model** packs one site's observations around a small circle: sky cover by how much of the circle is filled, temperature upper left, dew point lower left, and coded sea level pressure upper right, where 148 means 1014.8 mb and 958 means 995.8 mb. The wind barb staff points in the direction the wind blows **from**; a full barb is 10 knots, a half barb 5, a pennant 50.

A **front** is the boundary where two air masses meet, and the weather comes from how the warm air gets lifted.

| Front | Symbol | Weather it brings |
|---|---|---|
| Cold | Blue line, triangles pointing the way it moves | Cold air wedges under warm air and lifts it steeply: a narrow band of showers or thunderstorms, then quick clearing, cooler and drier, with a wind shift |
| Warm | Red line, half circles pointing the way it moves | Warm air rides up over retreating cold air: long hours of light steady rain, then warmer and more humid |
| Stationary | Blue triangles and red half circles alternating on opposite sides | Neither mass advances: days of clouds and light precipitation in one place |
| Occluded | Purple line, triangles and half circles on the same side | A cold front overtakes a warm front and lifts the warm air off the ground: widespread precipitation, usually a dying low |

**Trap:** Where contour lines cross a stream, the V points downstream in the direction the water flows. Actually the V points upstream. The stream occupies the lowest ground in the valley, so a contour must run up the valley before it can cross and come back, which aims the point of the V toward higher ground.

sections.h: Ocean currents and their effect on climate
sections.body:
**Surface currents** occupy roughly the top few hundred meters and are driven by the prevailing winds, then steered by the **Coriolis effect** and by the continents in the way. Because Earth's rotation deflects moving fluids to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, wind-driven water piles into **gyres**, huge circular systems that turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern. Warm currents generally run away from the equator along the western side of an ocean basin, and cold currents run back toward the equator along the eastern side.

**Deep currents** are driven by density, not wind, in what is called **thermohaline circulation** from the Greek for heat and salt. Cold water is denser than warm, and salty water is denser than fresh, so the coldest saltiest water is heaviest and sinks. That happens mainly in the far North Atlantic and around Antarctica, where surface water chills and, as sea ice forms, leaves its salt behind in the water below. The sunken water creeps along the bottom and rises slowly elsewhere, a global loop that takes on the order of a thousand years.

| Current | Type | Where | Climate effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift | Warm | North along the US east coast, then northeast across the Atlantic | Mild winters in Ireland, Britain, and Norway compared with the same latitude in Canada |
| California Current | Cold | South along the US west coast | Cool summers, coastal fog, a dry coastal climate |
| Peru (Humboldt) Current | Cold, with strong upwelling | North along western South America | Cool dry coast and one of the world's richest fisheries |

The **Gulf Stream** carries warm water out of the Gulf of Mexico through the Straits of Florida, north along the coast, then east as the North Atlantic Drift. It moves an enormous amount of tropical heat, and the prevailing westerlies blow across it on their way to Europe, which is why northwestern Europe is far milder than land at the same latitude elsewhere.

**Upwelling** happens where wind pushes surface water away from a coast and cold water rises to replace it. That deep water is loaded with nutrients from material that sank and decomposed, so it fertilizes plankton blooms. Upwelling zones cover a small fraction of the ocean but supply an outsized share of the world's fish catch.

In **El Nino** the Pacific trade winds weaken, warm water that normally piles up in the western Pacific slides back east, and upwelling off South America shuts down, collapsing the anchovy fishery and shifting rainfall worldwide. **La Nina** is the opposite: stronger trades, colder and more vigorous eastern Pacific upwelling. For Florida, El Nino winters tend to be cooler, wetter, and stormier, while the Atlantic hurricane season is usually quieter because stronger upper winds shear storms apart. La Nina winters tend to be warmer and drier, raising spring wildfire risk, and hurricane seasons tend to be more active.

Currents matter for climate because water resists temperature change. Its specific heat is far higher than soil or rock, so a coastal town warms and cools slowly and swings through a much smaller daily and yearly temperature range than an inland town at the same latitude. Globally, currents and winds together carry surplus heat from the tropics toward the poles; without that transport the tropics would be far hotter and the high latitudes far colder.

**Trap:** Deep ocean currents are just slower versions of surface currents, pushed along by the same winds. Actually wind drives only the upper few hundred meters. Below that, motion is driven by density differences set by temperature and salinity, which is why the deep circulation begins where surface water gets cold and salty enough to sink.

sections.h: Earth's motions: day, year, seasons, and tilt
sections.body:
**Rotation** is Earth spinning on its axis, once about every 24 hours, producing day and night. **Revolution** is Earth orbiting the Sun, once about every 365.25 days, producing the year. The extra quarter day is why we insert a leap day every four years.

Seasons are caused by the **23.5 degree tilt** of Earth's axis, which stays pointed in the same direction in space as Earth orbits. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it receives sunlight at a higher angle and for more hours per day, so it gets more energy per unit area: summer. The Southern Hemisphere is simultaneously in winter.

| Event | Approximate date | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| June solstice | June 21 | Northern Hemisphere summer begins, longest N day |
| September equinox | September 22 | Day and night nearly equal everywhere |
| December solstice | December 21 | Northern Hemisphere winter begins, shortest N day |
| March equinox | March 20 | Day and night nearly equal everywhere |

Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, and Earth is actually **closest** to the Sun in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter. That fact alone disproves the distance explanation for seasons.

The tilt also explains why the tropics have little seasonal temperature variation while high latitudes have extreme variation, and why the poles get 24 hours of daylight or darkness at the solstices.
