**Trap:** Seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer and farther in winter. Actually Earth's distance from the Sun varies only about 3 percent, and the Northern Hemisphere summer occurs when Earth is farthest away. Seasons come from axial tilt changing the angle of incoming sunlight and the length of daylight. If distance caused seasons, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time, and they do not.

The Moon does not produce light; we see reflected sunlight. Half the Moon is always lit; phases depend on how much of the lit half faces Earth. One full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.

[[diagram:moon]]

Order of phases starting from new moon:

| Phase | Appearance | Position relative to Sun and Earth |
|---|---|---|
| New | Not visible | Between Earth and Sun |
| Waxing crescent | Thin sliver, lit on right (N. Hemisphere) | Moving east of Sun |
| First quarter | Right half lit | 90 degrees from Sun |
| Waxing gibbous | More than half, growing | Approaching opposition |
| Full | Fully lit | Earth between Sun and Moon |
| Waning gibbous | More than half, shrinking | Past opposition |
| Third (last) quarter | Left half lit | 90 degrees on other side |
| Waning crescent | Thin sliver, lit on left | Approaching new |

Waxing means growing, waning means shrinking. Crescent is less than half lit; gibbous is more than half.

The Moon is in **synchronous rotation**: its rotation period equals its orbital period, so the same side always faces Earth. There is no permanently dark side; the far side receives just as much sunlight, it just faces away from us.

**Eclipses.** A **solar** eclipse happens at new moon when the Moon passes between Sun and Earth and casts a shadow on Earth. A **lunar** eclipse happens at full moon when Earth passes between Sun and Moon and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Eclipses are not monthly because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees, so alignment is usually imperfect.

**Tides** result from the Moon's gravitational pull, with a smaller solar contribution. Two high and two low tides occur roughly each day. **Spring tides** (largest range) occur at new and full moon when Sun and Moon align. **Neap tides** (smallest range) occur at the quarter phases.

**Trap:** Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. Actually Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, a rare event. Phases are simply our changing viewing angle on the always half-lit Moon.

sections.h: The solar system: planets and small bodies
sections.body:
The solar system formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. The Sun holds over 99 percent of the system's mass.

Order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Mnemonic: "My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles."

| Group | Members | Traits |
|---|---|---|
| Terrestrial (inner) | Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars | Small, rocky, dense, few or no moons, no rings, slow rotation |
| Gas and ice giants (outer) | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune | Large, low density, thick atmospheres, many moons, rings, fast rotation |

Signature facts: Mercury has extreme temperature swings and no real atmosphere. Venus has a runaway greenhouse from a dense CO2 atmosphere and is the hottest planet, hotter than Mercury despite being farther out. Mars has the largest volcano and canyon system in the solar system and polar ice. Jupiter is the most massive planet with the Great Red Spot. Saturn has the most prominent rings and the lowest density of any planet, less than water. Uranus rotates on its side, tilted about 98 degrees. Neptune has the strongest measured winds.

Small bodies: the **asteroid belt** lies between Mars and Jupiter. **Comets** are ice and dust bodies from the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud that grow tails when solar heating vaporizes ice. A **meteoroid** is a rock in space; a **meteor** is the streak of light as it burns in the atmosphere; a **meteorite** is the piece that reaches the ground. Pluto was reclassified in 2006 as a dwarf planet because it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood.

Kepler's laws: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus; a planet moves faster when nearer the Sun; more distant planets take longer to orbit.

**Trap:** Mercury is the hottest planet because it is closest to the Sun. Actually Venus is hotter, around 465 degrees C at the surface, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps enormous amounts of heat. Mercury has almost no atmosphere and so radiates its heat away at night.

sections.h: Stars: energy, classification, and life cycles
sections.body:
A star is a self-gravitating ball of plasma that fuses light nuclei into heavier ones in its core, converting a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy. In the Sun, hydrogen fuses to helium in the proton-proton chain.

```
E = m * c^2
E = energy released (J)
m = mass converted (kg)
c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s
```

**Worked example.** Converting just 1.0 kg of mass entirely to energy yields E = (1.0)(3.00 x 10^8)^2 = 9.0 x 10^16 J, comparable to the annual electricity use of a large city. This is why stars shine for billions of years.

Stars are classified by surface temperature into spectral types **O, B, A, F, G, K, M**, hottest to coolest, remembered as "Oh, Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me." O stars are blue and can exceed 30,000 K; M stars are red and are cooler than about 3,500 K. Our Sun is a G-type yellow star at roughly 5,800 K surface temperature. Color therefore indicates temperature: blue is hot, red is cool.

The **Hertzsprung-Russell diagram** plots luminosity against temperature. Most stars, including the Sun, lie on the main sequence band. Red giants sit above and to the right (bright but cool), white dwarfs below and to the left (hot but dim).

Life cycle depends on mass. All stars begin in a nebula, contract into a protostar, and reach the main sequence. A Sun-like star then becomes a red giant, sheds a planetary nebula, and ends as a white dwarf. A star much more massive becomes a supergiant, explodes as a **supernova**, and leaves a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole. Massive stars live shorter lives despite more fuel, because they burn it far faster.

Elements heavier than helium were forged in stars and scattered by supernovae, which is the literal origin of the carbon and iron in your body.

**Trap:** Red stars are hotter than blue stars because we associate red with hot. Actually blue is hotter. Higher temperature shifts peak emission to shorter wavelengths, toward blue.

sections.h: Galaxies, the universe, and space exploration
sections.body:
The Sun is one of a few hundred billion stars in the **Milky Way**, a barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across, with the solar system roughly 26,000 light-years from the center. Galaxies come in spiral, elliptical, and irregular forms and cluster into groups, clusters, and superclusters.

Distances need appropriate units:

| Unit | Definition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Astronomical unit (AU) | Average Earth to Sun distance, about 1.5 x 10^11 m | Within the solar system |
| Light-year (ly) | Distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 x 10^15 m | Stars and nearby galaxies |
| Parsec | About 3.26 light-years | Professional astronomy |

A light-year is a unit of **distance**, not time. Because light takes time to arrive, looking at distant objects means looking into the past: sunlight is about 8.3 minutes old when it reaches Earth.

The **Big Bang** model holds that the observable universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. Three main lines of evidence support it: the redshift of distant galaxies showing that space is expanding, with more distant galaxies receding faster (Hubble's observation); the cosmic microwave background radiation, a nearly uniform faint glow left from the early hot universe; and the observed abundances of hydrogen and helium, which match predictions of early nucleosynthesis.

Space exploration tools and why each exists: ground telescopes are large and cheap but must look through turbulent, absorbing atmosphere; space telescopes such as Hubble and Webb see wavelengths blocked by the atmosphere and get sharper images; probes and rovers make direct measurements; and spectroscopy lets us determine composition, temperature, and motion of objects we can never visit.

**Trap:** The Big Bang was an explosion of matter into empty space, from a center we could point to. Actually it was an expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once. There is no center and no edge to point at; every observer sees distant galaxies receding from their own position.

sections.h: Characteristics of life and levels of organization
sections.body:
All living things share a set of characteristics, and the exam expects you to apply them to edge cases. Living things are made of cells, use energy through metabolism, grow and develop, respond to stimuli, maintain homeostasis, reproduce, and evolve as populations over generations.

Viruses fail this list: they have no cells, no metabolism of their own, and cannot reproduce without hijacking a host, which is why most biologists do not classify them as alive.

Levels of biological organization, smallest to largest:

| Level | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Atom | Basic unit of an element | Carbon |
| Molecule | Bonded atoms | Glucose |
| Organelle | Structure inside a cell | Mitochondrion |
| Cell | Smallest unit of life | Muscle cell |
| Tissue | Similar cells with a shared job | Cardiac muscle tissue |
| Organ | Tissues working together | Heart |
| Organ system | Organs working together | Circulatory system |
| Organism | One complete individual | One human |
| Population | Same species, same area | All manatees in a spring |
| Community | All populations in an area | Manatees, seagrass, fish |
| Ecosystem | Community plus abiotic factors | The spring with its water and rock |
| Biome | Regional ecosystem type | Subtropical wetland |
| Biosphere | All life on Earth | Earth |

**Homeostasis** is maintaining stable internal conditions despite external change. Human examples: sweating and shivering to hold body temperature near 37 degrees C, insulin and glucagon to hold blood glucose steady, kidneys regulating water and salt, and breathing rate adjusting to blood carbon dioxide. Most homeostasis uses **negative feedback**, where the response reverses the change. Childbirth contractions and blood clotting are the classic **positive feedback** exceptions, where the response amplifies the change until an endpoint.

**Trap:** Homeostasis means internal conditions never change. Actually conditions oscillate constantly within a narrow tolerable range. Homeostasis is active regulation around a set point, not perfect stillness.

The **cell theory** has three parts: all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things, and all cells come from preexisting cells.

[[diagram:cell]]

**Prokaryotes** (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, have a cell wall, are small, and carry a circular chromosome in the cytoplasm. **Eukaryotes** (plants, animals, fungi, protists) have a true nucleus and many membrane-bound organelles, and are larger and more complex. Both have DNA, ribosomes, cytoplasm, and a plasma membrane.

| Organelle | Function | Where found |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | Houses DNA, directs the cell | Eukaryotes |
| Ribosome | Builds proteins | All cells |
| Mitochondrion | Cellular respiration, makes ATP | Plant and animal |
| Chloroplast | Photosynthesis, holds chlorophyll | Plant and algae only |
| Rough ER | Protein processing, studded with ribosomes | Eukaryotes |
| Smooth ER | Lipid synthesis, detoxification | Eukaryotes |
| Golgi apparatus | Modifies, sorts, ships proteins | Eukaryotes |
| Lysosome | Digests waste with enzymes | Mostly animal |
| Vacuole | Storage; large central one gives plants turgor | Large in plants |
| Cell wall | Rigid support, made of cellulose in plants | Plants, fungi, bacteria |
| Cell membrane | Selective barrier, phospholipid bilayer | All cells |
| Cytoskeleton | Shape, internal transport | Eukaryotes |

Plant cells have chloroplasts, a cell wall, and a large central vacuole. Animal cells have centrioles and lysosomes and usually a more flexible shape. Both have nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi, and membrane.

A useful analogy: the nucleus is the main office, ribosomes are the assembly line, mitochondria are the power plant, the Golgi is shipping and receiving, and the membrane is security at the door.

**Trap:** Plant cells do not have mitochondria because they have chloroplasts instead. Actually plant cells have both. Chloroplasts capture light energy to make glucose; mitochondria then break glucose down to release ATP, which plants need day and night.

The cell membrane is a **phospholipid bilayer** with embedded proteins, and it is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and blocks others. Transport falls into two families based on whether the cell spends ATP.

**Passive transport** requires no energy and moves substances down a concentration gradient, from high to low, driven by random molecular motion.

| Type | What moves | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Simple diffusion | Small nonpolar molecules, O2, CO2 | Straight through the bilayer |
| Facilitated diffusion | Glucose, ions | Through a channel or carrier protein, still downhill |
| Osmosis | Water | Across a semipermeable membrane toward higher solute concentration |

**Active transport** requires ATP and moves substances against the gradient, from low to high. The sodium-potassium pump is the standard example. **Endocytosis** brings large material in by engulfing it in a vesicle (phagocytosis for solids), and **exocytosis** expels material.

Solution tonicity governs cell behavior in water:

| Solution | Solute outside vs. inside | Water net movement | Effect on animal cell |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hypotonic | Less solute outside | Into the cell | Swells, may burst (lysis) |
| Isotonic | Equal | No net movement | Stays the same |
| Hypertonic | More solute outside | Out of the cell | Shrinks (crenation); plant cell plasmolyzes and wilts |

**Worked reasoning example.** A plant is watered with heavily salted water. The soil solution becomes hypertonic to root cells, so water moves out of the roots, cells lose turgor pressure, and the plant wilts even though liquid water surrounds it. This is also why saltwater intrusion kills freshwater vegetation.

Surface area to volume ratio limits cell size. As a cell grows, volume increases faster than surface area, so at some point the membrane cannot supply the interior. That is why cells stay small and why absorptive structures have folds and villi.

**Trap:** In osmosis, water moves from low concentration to high concentration, which violates diffusion. Actually water still moves down its own gradient, from where water is more concentrated to where water is less concentrated. That is the same place as high solute concentration, so both statements describe one process.

These two processes are near mirror images and together move energy through nearly every ecosystem. Photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose bonds; respiration releases it as ATP.

```
Photosynthesis:
6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light energy  gives  C6H12O6 + 6 O2
Site: chloroplast. Reactants: carbon dioxide, water, light.
Products: glucose, oxygen. Endothermic, stores energy.

Aerobic cellular respiration:
C6H12O6 + 6 O2  gives  6 CO2 + 6 H2O + ATP (about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose)
Site: cytoplasm (glycolysis) then mitochondrion (Krebs cycle, electron transport chain).
Exothermic, releases energy.
```

Photosynthesis has two stages. **Light-dependent reactions** occur in the thylakoid membranes, split water, release oxygen as a byproduct, and produce ATP and NADPH. The **Calvin cycle** (light-independent) occurs in the stroma and uses that ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue wavelengths and reflects green, which is why leaves look green.

Respiration without oxygen is **fermentation**, which yields only about 2 ATP per glucose. Lactic acid fermentation happens in muscle during hard exercise; alcoholic fermentation in yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is what leavens bread.

**ATP** is the cell's usable energy currency. Energy is released when the bond to the third phosphate breaks, converting ATP to ADP plus a free phosphate.

Limiting factors for photosynthesis: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature, and water availability. Raise one while another is limiting and the rate does not improve, which is a common experimental design question.

**Trap:** Plants photosynthesize during the day and respire only at night. Actually plants perform cellular respiration continuously, day and night. During daylight photosynthesis usually outpaces respiration, so there is net oxygen release, which masks the ongoing respiration.

**Mitosis** produces two genetically identical diploid cells from one, for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. **Meiosis** produces four genetically different haploid gametes from one diploid cell, for sexual reproduction.

The cell cycle: interphase (G1 growth, S phase DNA replication, G2 preparation), then mitosis, then cytokinesis. Most of a cell's life is interphase.

Phases of mitosis, in order, remembered as **PMAT**:

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| Prophase | Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes; nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle forms |
| Metaphase | Chromosomes line up single file on the cell's midline (equator) |
| Anaphase | Sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles |
| Telophase | Two nuclei re-form; chromosomes unwind |
| Cytokinesis | Cytoplasm divides; animal cells pinch with a cleavage furrow, plant cells build a cell plate |

| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Divisions | One | Two (meiosis I and II) |
| Daughter cells | 2 | 4 |
| Chromosome number | Diploid, same as parent (2n) | Haploid, half of parent (n) |
| Genetic result | Identical | Genetically unique |
| Crossing over | No | Yes, in prophase I |
| Purpose | Growth and repair | Gamete production |

In humans, body cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), and gametes are haploid with 23. Fertilization restores 46.

Two sources of variation in meiosis: **crossing over** during prophase I, where homologous chromosomes swap segments, and **independent assortment** during metaphase I, where each homologous pair orients randomly. Random fertilization adds a third.

Uncontrolled mitosis is the basis of cancer, which arises when the checkpoints regulating the cell cycle fail.

**Trap:** Meiosis makes cells identical to the parent, just with half the chromosomes. Actually crossing over and independent assortment make each of the four products genetically unique. That variation is the raw material natural selection acts on.

DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. Each nucleotide has a phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar, and one of four nitrogen bases. Base pairing is strict and worth memorizing: in DNA, adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine. In RNA, uracil replaces thymine, so adenine pairs with uracil.

| Feature | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Strands | Double | Single |
| Sugar | Deoxyribose | Ribose |
| Bases | A, T, G, C | A, U, G, C |
| Location | Nucleus mainly | Nucleus and cytoplasm |
| Role | Stores genetic information | Carries and interprets it |

The central dogma runs DNA to RNA to protein.

**Replication** copies DNA semiconservatively: the helix unzips and each strand serves as a template, so each new molecule has one old and one new strand. **Transcription** happens in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase builds mRNA from a DNA template. **Translation** happens at the ribosome, where tRNA brings amino acids matching each three-base mRNA codon, and the amino acids link into a polypeptide.

**Worked example.** A DNA template strand reads TAC GGA. The mRNA transcribed from it reads AUG CCU. AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine; CCU codes for proline.

**Worked example 2.** If a DNA sample is 30 percent adenine, then thymine is also 30 percent, leaving 40 percent split evenly between guanine and cytosine, so 20 percent each.

**Mutations** are changes in the DNA sequence. Substitutions swap one base and may be silent, may change one amino acid, or may create a premature stop. Insertions and deletions of a number of bases not divisible by three cause a **frameshift**, which usually ruins the whole downstream protein and so is often more damaging. Only mutations in gametes are inherited.

**Trap:** Every mutation is harmful and causes disease. Actually most mutations are neutral, some are silent because of redundancy in the genetic code, and a few are beneficial. Beneficial mutations are the source of new variation for evolution.

A **gene** is a segment of DNA coding for a trait; an **allele** is a version of that gene. **Genotype** is the allele pair; **phenotype** is the observable trait. **Homozygous** means two identical alleles (BB or bb); **heterozygous** means two different ones (Bb). A **dominant** allele masks a recessive one in a heterozygote.

[[diagram:punnett]]

Mendel's principles: the law of segregation (allele pairs separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets one) and the law of independent assortment (genes on different chromosomes are inherited independently).

**Worked Punnett square.** Cross two heterozygous tall pea plants, Tt x Tt.

| | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | TT | Tt |
| **t** | Tt | tt |

Genotype ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Phenotype ratio 3 tall : 1 short, so 75 percent tall and 25 percent short.

**Worked example 2.** A test cross of Tt x tt gives Tt, Tt, tt, tt: 50 percent tall and 50 percent short.

Non-Mendelian patterns to distinguish:

| Pattern | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Incomplete dominance | Heterozygote is a blend | Red x white snapdragon gives pink |
| Codominance | Both alleles fully expressed, side by side | Roan cattle; human AB blood type |
| Multiple alleles | More than two alleles in the population | ABO blood groups |
| Polygenic | Many genes, continuous range | Human height, skin color |
| Sex-linked | Gene on the X chromosome | Colorblindness, hemophilia |

Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus one sex pair: XX female, XY male. Because males have only one X, X-linked recessive conditions appear far more often in males, and a carrier mother can pass the allele to sons.

A **pedigree** traces inheritance across generations; squares are males, circles are females, and shaded shapes show the trait.

**Trap:** Dominant traits are the most common traits in a population, and recessive ones are rare. Actually dominance describes only which allele is expressed in a heterozygote, not frequency. Polydactyly is dominant and rare; having five fingers per hand is recessive at that locus and nearly universal.

Evolution is change in the heritable characteristics of populations over generations. Natural selection is the primary mechanism, and Darwin's logic has four steps: there is heritable variation in a population, organisms produce more offspring than can survive, individuals with traits better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, and therefore those traits become more common over generations.

Selection acts on existing variation; it does not create traits on demand. Populations evolve, individuals do not. An individual giraffe cannot evolve a longer neck in its lifetime.

Lines of evidence:

| Evidence type | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Fossil record | Sequences of change over time, transitional forms |
| Comparative anatomy | Homologous structures from common ancestry (whale flipper, bat wing, human arm); vestigial structures |
| Comparative embryology | Similar early developmental stages in related groups |
| Molecular biology | Shared DNA and protein sequences, universal genetic code |
| Biogeography | Related species on adjacent landmasses, island radiations |
| Direct observation | Antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance, Galapagos finch beak change |

Distinguish **homologous** structures (same underlying structure, common ancestry, possibly different function) from **analogous** structures (similar function evolved independently, as in insect and bird wings, which is convergent evolution).

Other mechanisms of evolutionary change: genetic drift (random change, strong in small populations), gene flow (migration), mutation (the ultimate source of new alleles), and sexual selection. **Speciation** usually requires reproductive isolation, often geographic separation. Selection types include directional, stabilizing, and disruptive.

**Trap:** Organisms evolve traits because they need them, and antibiotic use causes bacteria to become resistant. Actually resistant mutants arise randomly before exposure. The antibiotic then kills the susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to multiply. Selection filters existing variation rather than generating it on demand. Saying an animal evolved a feature in order to survive reverses the causation.

Two clusters of factual material recur on this exam: organ systems and taxonomy.

| System | Primary function | Key organs |
|---|---|---|
| Digestive | Break down food, absorb nutrients | Mouth, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestine, liver, pancreas |
| Respiratory | Gas exchange | Nose, trachea, bronchi, lungs, alveoli, diaphragm |
| Circulatory | Transport blood, oxygen, nutrients | Heart, arteries, veins, capillaries |
| Nervous | Detect stimuli, coordinate response | Brain, spinal cord, nerves |
| Endocrine | Hormonal regulation | Pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas |
| Muscular | Movement | Skeletal, smooth, cardiac muscle |
| Skeletal | Support, protection, blood cell production | Bones, cartilage, ligaments |
| Excretory | Remove wastes, balance water | Kidneys, bladder, ureters, urethra |
| Immune or lymphatic | Defend against pathogens | Lymph nodes, spleen, white blood cells |
| Integumentary | Barrier, temperature regulation | Skin, hair, nails |
| Reproductive | Produce offspring | Ovaries, uterus, testes |

Systems interact constantly. The respiratory system loads oxygen onto blood that the circulatory system delivers to muscle, where mitochondria use it in respiration; the nervous system sets the breathing rate based on blood carbon dioxide. Digestive and circulatory systems partner to distribute glucose.

Taxonomy, broadest to narrowest: **Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.** Mnemonic: "Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup." Organisms in the same genus are more closely related than organisms that share only a class.

**Binomial nomenclature** from Linnaeus gives each species a two-part Latin name, genus capitalized and species lowercase, both italicized or underlined: Homo sapiens, Karenia brevis.

The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. Eukarya includes the kingdoms Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia.

**Trap:** Two organisms in the same family are more closely related than two in the same genus. Actually genus is narrower than family, so sharing a genus indicates a closer relationship. The categories get more specific and more closely related as you move from domain toward species.

A vascular plant has three organs. **Roots** anchor it, absorb water and dissolved minerals, and store food; root hairs multiply the absorbing surface enormously. **Stems** hold leaves up to the light and house the transport tissue, and some store food (a white potato is a swollen stem, not a root). **Leaves** are the photosynthesis factory: a broad blade to catch light, veins for plumbing, pores for gas exchange.

Two tissues do the transport. **Xylem** carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots **upward only**, through cells that are dead and hollow at maturity, essentially pipes. **Phloem** carries sugar made in the leaves to wherever it is used or stored, up or down, through living cells. Memory hook: **ph**loem carries **ph**ood, and food travels both ways; xylem is the other one, water, and only up.

Water rises without any pump. Evaporation from the leaves, called **transpiration**, pulls on the water column, and because water molecules cling to each other by hydrogen bonding (cohesion) and to the xylem walls (adhesion), the whole thread is drawn up from the roots. That is the transpiration pull, and the Sun does the work. Most of the water a plant takes up leaves again this way.

Transpiration happens through **stomata**, pores mostly on the underside of the leaf, each flanked by two **guard cells**. When guard cells take in water and swell, they bow apart and the pore opens; when they lose water and go limp, it closes. That is the plant's central trade-off: an open stoma lets carbon dioxide in but lets water vapor out, so in heat or drought the plant closes up and photosynthesis slows. The **cuticle**, a waxy layer the epidermis secretes over leaves and stems, blocks water loss everywhere else and is thickest in desert plants. Because it seals the surface, essentially all gas exchange must go through the stomata.

**Nonvascular plants** (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) have no xylem or phloem and no true roots, stems, or leaves. They stay small and low, live in damp places, and need a film of water for sperm to reach eggs. **Vascular plants** have conducting tissue stiffened with lignin, so they stand tall and tolerate drier ground. Ferns reproduce by spores; seed plants split in two. **Gymnosperms** ("naked seed") bear seeds on cones, with no flower and no fruit, are mostly wind pollinated, and include pines, cypresses, and cycads. **Angiosperms** are the flowering plants, whose seeds develop inside a fruit, the ripened ovary.

In a flower, the male **stamen** is an **anther** that makes pollen on a stalk, the **filament**. The female **pistil** is a sticky **stigma** that catches pollen, a **style**, and an **ovary** holding the ovules. **Petals** advertise to pollinators; **sepals** protected the bud before it opened. **Pollination** transfers pollen from anther to stigma by wind, water, insects, birds, or bats. A pollen tube then grows down the style, each fertilized ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes the fruit. **Seed dispersal** carries offspring away from competition with the parent: wind (dandelion, maple samara), water (coconut, mangrove propagule), animals (burrs on fur, fruit eaten and passed), and explosive release.

A **tropism** is growth toward or away from a stimulus. The response is a permanent bend in the growing tissue, not a movement.

| Tropism | Stimulus | Shoots | Roots |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phototropism | Light | Grow toward it (positive) | Grow away from it (negative) |
| Gravitropism (geotropism) | Gravity | Grow upward, against the pull (negative) | Grow downward, with the pull (positive) |
| Thigmotropism | Touch or contact | Tendrils and twining stems coil around a support (positive) | Grow away from an obstacle |

Tropisms are run by **plant hormones**. **Auxin** promotes cell elongation, collects on the shaded side of a stem, and enforces apical dominance. Also name gibberellins (stem elongation, germination), cytokinins (cell division), ethylene (a gas that ripens fruit), and abscisic acid (closes stomata under water stress).

**Trap:** A plant bends toward light because the cells on the lit side grow faster in the extra sunlight. Actually it is the shaded side that grows faster. Auxin migrates away from the light, accumulates on the dark side, and makes those cells elongate more, which pushes the stem over so the tip leans toward the light.

title: Knowledge of the effects of physical and biological factors on the environment

sections.h: Ecosystem structure: biotic and abiotic factors
sections.body:
An **ecosystem** is all the living things in an area plus the nonliving conditions they interact with. **Biotic** factors are living or once-living: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, dead leaves. **Abiotic** factors are nonliving: sunlight, temperature, water, soil, pH, salinity, dissolved oxygen, wind, and nutrients.

A **habitat** is where an organism lives; a **niche** is its full role, including what it eats, when it is active, where it nests, and how it interacts. Two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same place indefinitely; one outcompetes the other or they partition resources.

A **limiting factor** is the resource in shortest supply that caps population growth. In a lake it might be phosphorus; in a forest understory, light; in a desert, water. **Carrying capacity** is the maximum population an environment can sustain given its limiting factors.

Population growth patterns: **exponential** growth produces a J-shaped curve when resources are unlimited, which cannot last. **Logistic** growth produces an S-shaped curve that levels off at carrying capacity as density-dependent factors kick in. Density-dependent limits include disease, competition, and predation; density-independent limits include hurricanes, freezes, and fire.

**Worked example.** A population of 100 rabbits grows 20 percent per year. After one year: 100 x 1.20 = 120. After two years: 120 x 1.20 = 144. After three years: 144 x 1.20 = about 173. The increase per year gets larger even though the percentage is constant, which is the signature of exponential growth.

**Ecological succession** is directional community change. **Primary succession** starts on bare rock or new lava with no soil, and pioneer species such as lichens begin soil formation. **Secondary succession** follows a disturbance that leaves soil intact, such as fire or abandoned farmland, and proceeds much faster.

**Trap:** Ecological succession always ends in a stable, permanent climax forest. Actually many ecosystems are maintained in earlier stages by recurring disturbance, and modern ecology treats communities as dynamic rather than fixed. Florida scrub and longleaf pine persist only because fire keeps resetting them.

sections.h: Energy flow: food chains, webs, and pyramids
sections.body:
Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, is captured by producers, and passes to consumers, losing usable energy at every step. Unlike matter, energy is not recycled; it flows one way and exits as heat.

[[diagram:pyramid]]

| Trophic level | Role | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Producers (autotrophs) | Make their own food | Plants, algae, cyanobacteria, chemosynthetic bacteria |
| Primary consumers | Herbivores | Grasshopper, manatee, deer |
| Secondary consumers | Eat herbivores | Frog, small fish, snake |
| Tertiary consumers | Eat secondary consumers | Hawk, alligator, shark |
| Decomposers | Break down dead matter, recycle nutrients | Bacteria, fungi, earthworms |

Arrows in a food chain always point in the direction energy moves, that is from the eaten to the eater. Grass to grasshopper to frog to snake to hawk.

The **ten percent rule**: roughly 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level is stored as biomass available to the next. The other 90 percent is lost to respiration, movement, heat, and undigested waste.

```
Energy at next level = 0.10 * energy at current level
(energy measured in J or kJ, or kcal)
```

**Worked example.** Producers capture 20,000 kJ. Primary consumers get about 2,000 kJ, secondary consumers about 200 kJ, tertiary consumers about 20 kJ. This is why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels and why top predators are always relatively few.

An **energy pyramid** is always widest at the bottom, because energy decreases upward. **Biomagnification** is the opposite pattern: persistent toxins such as mercury and DDT concentrate at higher trophic levels, which is why large predatory fish carry the greatest mercury burden.

A **food web** is more realistic than a chain because most organisms eat several things. Remove one species and effects ripple through multiple pathways. A **keystone species** has an outsized effect relative to its abundance, such as the alligator whose dry-season gator holes shelter many Everglades species.

**Trap:** Decomposers sit at the top of the food chain because they consume everything. Actually decomposers act on every level and return nutrients to the soil and water for producers, so they are best drawn as a cycle beside the pyramid, not as a top tier.

Matter, unlike energy, is recycled. Each cycle has reservoirs where the element is stored and processes that move it between them.

**Water cycle.** Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff, and groundwater flow, powered by the Sun and gravity.

**Carbon cycle.** Carbon dioxide is removed from air by photosynthesis and returned by cellular respiration, decomposition, combustion, and volcanic activity. Long-term reservoirs are limestone rock, fossil fuels, deep ocean water, and soil organic matter. The ocean absorbs a large share of atmospheric carbon dioxide, which lowers seawater pH: **ocean acidification**, a direct threat to shell and coral formation.

**Nitrogen cycle.** Nitrogen gas makes up 78 percent of air but plants cannot use N2 directly.

| Step | Process | Agent |
|---|---|---|
| Nitrogen fixation | N2 to ammonia or ammonium | Rhizobium bacteria in legume root nodules, cyanobacteria, lightning |
| Nitrification | Ammonium to nitrite to nitrate | Nitrifying bacteria |
| Assimilation | Plants take up nitrate | Plant roots |
| Ammonification | Wastes and dead tissue to ammonium | Decomposers |
| Denitrification | Nitrate back to N2 gas | Denitrifying bacteria in low-oxygen soil |

**Phosphorus cycle.** Unusual in having no significant atmospheric step. Phosphorus weathers out of rock, cycles through soil, water, and organisms, and settles into sediment. This matters in Florida, where mined phosphate rock becomes fertilizer and excess runoff drives algal blooms.

**Oxygen cycle.** Released by photosynthesis, consumed by respiration and combustion.

**Trap:** Plants get their nitrogen straight from the air, the way they get carbon dioxide. Actually the triple bond in N2 makes it inert to plants. Nitrogen must first be fixed into ammonium or nitrate by bacteria or lightning, which is why legumes and their root-nodule bacteria are so important in agriculture.

Organisms interact in patterned ways, and the exam expects you to name the relationship from a described scenario.

| Interaction | Effect on species 1 | Effect on species 2 | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutualism | Benefit | Benefit | Bee and flower; legume and Rhizobium; coral and zooxanthellae |
| Commensalism | Benefit | No significant effect | Barnacle on a whale; Spanish moss on an oak; remora and shark |
| Parasitism | Benefit | Harm, usually not immediate death | Tick on a deer; tapeworm in an intestine; mistletoe |
| Predation | Benefit | Killed | Alligator eating a fish |
| Competition | Harm | Harm | Two bird species contesting the same nest cavity |

**Symbiosis** is the umbrella term for a close, long-term relationship between two species, so mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism are all symbiotic. Predation and competition are interactions but are not usually classed as symbiosis.

Competition can be **interspecific** (between species) or **intraspecific** (within a species, often more intense because needs overlap completely). **Resource partitioning** reduces competition by dividing a resource, as when warblers feed at different heights in the same tree.

Defensive strategies to recognize: **camouflage** blends in, **mimicry** copies a dangerous or unpalatable model, and **warning coloration** advertises real toxicity. A viceroy butterfly resembling a monarch is mimicry; the coral snake's bands are warning coloration.

Predator and prey populations often oscillate together with the predator peak lagging the prey peak, because predators can only increase after prey become abundant, then crash the prey population and starve.

**Trap:** A parasite is just a very efficient predator, so parasitism and predation are the same relationship. Actually a predator kills prey quickly and typically consumes it; a parasite lives on or in a host over time and usually keeps the host alive, because a dead host is a dead home. A successful parasite is one that does not kill its host quickly.

A **biome** is a large region defined by its climate, especially temperature and precipitation, and by the community adapted to it. Latitude, elevation, and proximity to water determine which biome forms where.

| Biome | Climate | Vegetation | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tropical rainforest | Warm, very wet year round | Dense broadleaf canopy, layered | Highest biodiversity; poor thin soil |
| Savanna | Warm, seasonal rain | Grasses with scattered trees | Fire and grazing maintained |
| Desert | Under 25 cm precipitation per year | Succulents, deep-rooted shrubs | Large day to night temperature swing |
| Temperate grassland | Moderate rain, cold winters | Grasses | Deepest, richest soils; farmed heavily |
| Temperate deciduous forest | Four distinct seasons | Trees that drop leaves | Much of the eastern United States |
| Taiga (boreal forest) | Cold, long winter | Conifers | Largest land biome |
| Tundra | Very cold, low precipitation | Mosses, lichens, low shrubs | Permafrost; no trees |

Aquatic systems are classified by salinity and depth. **Freshwater** includes lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, and wetlands. **Marine** includes the intertidal zone, the shallow sunlit photic zone, the open ocean, coral reefs, and the deep aphotic zone. **Estuaries**, where fresh and salt water mix, are brackish, highly productive, and serve as nursery habitat for many marine species.

Light availability drives aquatic zonation: photosynthesis is limited to the upper photic zone, so producers, and therefore most life, concentrate near the surface or in shallow water. Deep-sea communities depend on sinking organic matter or, at hydrothermal vents, on chemosynthesis.

Wetlands, whether freshwater marsh, swamp, or mangrove, filter pollutants, store floodwater, recharge aquifers, and shelter juvenile fish.

**Trap:** Tropical rainforests must have the richest soil, since so much grows there. Actually rainforest soils are thin and nutrient poor. Nutrients are held in living biomass and recycled rapidly by decomposers, so cleared land loses fertility within a few growing seasons.

Florida-specific environmental content appears on this exam, so treat it as required material.

**The Everglades.** Historically a shallow sheet of fresh water roughly 60 miles wide moving slowly south from Lake Okeechobee to Florida Bay, the "river of grass," dominated by sawgrass with tree islands, cypress, and mangrove at the coast. Twentieth-century canals, levees, and the straightened Kissimmee River cut flow volume and altered timing, shrinking the wetland by about half. The Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan aims to restore more natural flow volume, timing, and water quality, including reservoirs, removing barriers, and Kissimmee re-meandering.

**Invasive species.** Non-native species that spread and cause harm, typically because they have no local predators, parasites, or competitors.

| Invader | Type | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Burmese python | Reptile, Everglades | Steep declines in marsh rabbits, raccoons, opossums, and other mammals |
| Lionfish | Marine fish, reefs | Voracious predator on juvenile reef fish, venomous spines, no natural predator here |
| Melaleuca | Tree, wetlands | Drinks heavily, forms dense stands, displaces sawgrass, alters fire behavior |
| Brazilian pepper | Shrub or tree | Dense thickets shading out natives across disturbed land |

**Red tide.** Blooms of the marine dinoflagellate Karenia brevis produce brevetoxins that kill fish, sicken marine mammals and birds, and cause respiratory irritation onshore. It occurs naturally in the Gulf but nutrient input can intensify and extend nearshore blooms.

**Manatees and seagrass.** Manatees graze seagrass. Nutrient pollution fuels algae that cloud the water and shade out seagrass beds, notably in the Indian River Lagoon, contributing to widespread manatee starvation events. Boat strikes and cold-water stress are additional pressures.

**Nutrient runoff and Lake Okeechobee.** Fertilizer, manure, and septic leachate carry nitrogen and phosphorus into waterways. Excess nutrients cause **eutrophication**: algae and cyanobacteria bloom, then die and decompose, and decomposers consume dissolved oxygen, producing hypoxic dead zones and fish kills. Okeechobee discharges can carry blooms into the Caloosahatchee and St. Lucie estuaries.

**Mangroves.** Red, black, and white mangroves stabilize shoreline sediment, blunt storm surge, filter runoff, and nurse juvenile fish, shrimp, and crab. Red mangrove prop roots sit lowest in the water; all are salt tolerant.

**Saltwater intrusion.** Heavy groundwater withdrawal and rising sea level push the freshwater to saltwater boundary inland within the porous limestone aquifer, threatening coastal wellfields, especially in southeast Florida.

**Fire-dependent longleaf pine.** Longleaf pine sandhill and flatwoods communities need frequent low-intensity fire. Fire clears hardwood competitors, opens the understory for wiregrass and many rare plants, and maintains habitat for gopher tortoise and red-cockaded woodpecker. Fire suppression, not fire, is the threat, which is why managers use prescribed burns.

**Coral bleaching in the Keys.** Corals host symbiotic zooxanthellae that supply most of their food. Prolonged heat stress makes corals expel the algae, turning white and starving. Ocean acidification, disease, and runoff compound the loss along the Florida Reef Tract.

**Hurricanes as natural disturbance.** Hurricanes damage reefs and coastal forests but also flush estuaries, redistribute sediment, open canopy gaps, and build barrier island dunes. They are part of the region's natural disturbance regime, and mangroves and dunes are the natural buffer.

**Trap:** Preventing all wildfire protects Florida's pine ecosystems. Actually longleaf pine communities are fire-dependent, and suppressing fire lets hardwoods and dense shrubs take over, eliminating the open habitat those species require and building fuel loads that make eventual fires far more destructive.

Human activity affects the environment through habitat loss, pollution, overharvest, invasive species introduction, and climate change. Habitat destruction and fragmentation are the leading causes of biodiversity loss worldwide.

**Air pollution.** Burning fossil fuels releases sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which react with water vapor to make **acid rain** (pH below about 5.0), damaging forests, leaching soil nutrients, and acidifying lakes. Vehicle exhaust plus sunlight makes ground-level ozone and photochemical smog. Particulate matter harms lungs. CFCs thinned the stratospheric ozone layer until the Montreal Protocol phased them out.

**Greenhouse effect and climate change.** Greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, and nitrous oxide, let visible sunlight through and absorb outgoing infrared, keeping Earth about 33 degrees C warmer than it would otherwise be. That natural effect makes life possible. The problem is **enhancement**: burning fossil fuels and clearing forests have raised atmospheric carbon dioxide sharply, increasing global average temperature, raising sea level through thermal expansion and ice melt, acidifying the ocean, and shifting precipitation patterns and species ranges.

**Water pollution.** Distinguish **point source** (a single identifiable outfall, such as a pipe from a plant) from **nonpoint source** (diffuse runoff from lawns, farms, roads, and construction). Nonpoint sources are harder to regulate and are the dominant problem in Florida.

**Conservation strategies.** Reduce, reuse, recycle, in that order of effectiveness, since reducing consumption prevents waste rather than processing it. Other approaches: protected lands and wildlife corridors, captive breeding, restoration ecology, integrated pest management, sustainable yield limits on fisheries, renewable energy, water conservation, and low-impact development that preserves infiltration.

**Trap:** The greenhouse effect is itself a form of pollution that we should try to eliminate. Actually the greenhouse effect is a natural and necessary process; without it Earth's average temperature would be well below freezing. The concern is the intensification of that effect by added greenhouse gases, not its existence.

title: Knowledge of the science learning environment

sections.h: Chemical safety law: OSHA HazCom, SDS, and labeling
sections.body:
School science labs fall under real occupational safety law, and exam items test whether you know the actual framework rather than generic caution.

**OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (HazCom), 29 CFR 1910.1200.** Often summarized as the right-to-know standard, it requires that every hazardous chemical in the workplace be identified and that employees have access to information about it. For a school, teachers and staff are the employees, and students working with those chemicals must be trained accordingly. HazCom is aligned with the Globally Harmonized System (GHS), which standardized labels and data sheets internationally.

**Safety Data Sheets (SDS).** Formerly called MSDS, an SDS is the manufacturer's hazard document for each chemical. Under GHS every SDS has the same 16 sections in the same order, so you always know where to look. Section 1 is identification, Section 2 hazard identification, Section 4 first aid measures, Section 7 handling and storage, Section 8 exposure controls and personal protective equipment, and Section 13 disposal. SDSs must be readily accessible to staff during all work shifts, not locked in an office someone else has the key to, and they should be reviewed **before** a chemical is used.

**Labeling.** Every container must be labeled. Manufacturer labels require the product identifier, signal word (Danger for more severe hazards, Warning for less severe), hazard statements, GHS pictograms, precautionary statements, and supplier information. Secondary containers, meaning anything a teacher pours chemical into, must also be labeled with the identity and hazards. Unlabeled containers are a violation and unknown contents must be treated as hazardous and handled by trained disposal personnel, never poured down a drain.

**Chemical hygiene plan.** OSHA's Laboratory Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1450, requires a written chemical hygiene plan for labs using hazardous chemicals. It documents standard operating procedures, required controls, PPE, ventilation and fume hood use, employee training, chemical inventory, storage and segregation of incompatible chemicals, spill and emergency procedures, waste disposal, and a designated chemical hygiene officer. The plan must be reviewed and updated at least annually and be available to employees.

Proper storage means segregating incompatibles: acids apart from bases, oxidizers apart from flammables and organics, flammables in an approved flammables cabinet, and nothing corrosive stored above shoulder height.

**Trap:** Safety Data Sheets are paperwork to file in case of an inspection. Actually the SDS is a working document to consult before you use a chemical and during an emergency, and OSHA requires it be immediately accessible to everyone working with the material.

sections.h: Engineering controls and personal protective equipment
sections.body:
Safety is layered. The strongest protection is to remove the hazard, then to control it with equipment, then to rely on personal gear. Relying only on goggles when a fume hood was the right answer is a design failure.

**Eye protection.** Florida, like most states, requires appropriate eye protection for teachers, students, and visitors whenever there is risk of injury from chemicals, heat, hot liquids, glassware, or flying particles. Choose the right type: safety glasses with side shields for impact and particles, **chemical splash goggles** that seal around the eyes for any liquid chemical work, and a face shield worn **over** goggles when the risk extends to the whole face. Ordinary prescription eyeglasses are not eye protection. Goggles must be sanitized between users, and eye protection is worn until all work in the room is finished, not just during your own pour.

**Eyewash and safety shower.** Any area where corrosives or other injurious chemicals are used needs an eyewash station and, where whole-body exposure is possible, a drench shower. Under the widely applied ANSI Z358.1 guidance, the unit must be reachable within about 10 seconds of unobstructed travel and roughly 55 feet, deliver tepid flushing fluid hands-free once activated, and be flushed and inspected weekly with a documented annual performance check. Flush eyes for a full 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, and remove contact lenses. Never block access to an eyewash with carts, stools, or storage.

**Other required equipment.** A fume hood for volatile or toxic vapors, working with the sash at the proper height. A properly rated fire extinguisher, most commonly ABC in a classroom, plus a fire blanket. A first aid kit. Chemical-resistant gloves matched to the chemical, since not every glove resists every substance. A lab apron. Sharps and broken-glass containers separate from regular trash. Clearly marked exits and a shutoff for gas and electricity.

Standard rules: no food or drink in a lab, no working alone or unsupervised, no unauthorized experiments, tie back long hair and secure loose clothing, closed-toe shoes, wash hands after, and know where every piece of safety equipment is before the activity starts.

**Trap:** Wearing gloves always makes chemical handling safer. Actually the wrong glove material can absorb a chemical and hold it against the skin, and gloves give false confidence and spread contamination to doorknobs and keyboards. Match glove material to the chemical using the SDS, and remove gloves before touching shared surfaces.

sections.h: Live organisms, dissection, and lower-hazard substitution
sections.body:
Working with living things and with animal tissue carries both ethical and safety obligations, and the exam expects the professional standard rather than personal preference.

**Live organism care.** A teacher who keeps organisms accepts responsibility for humane housing, appropriate food and water, clean conditions, suitable temperature and light, and a plan for weekends, holidays, and the end of the school year. Never release classroom organisms into the wild, since that spreads disease and can create invasive populations, a serious concern in Florida. Handle animals gently and minimally, wash hands before and after, and be alert to allergies. Do not use venomous animals, wild-caught mammals, or birds. Reptiles, amphibians, and baby chicks carry Salmonella risk, so hand hygiene is not optional. Living cultures such as bacteria should use known, nonpathogenic strains, be grown in sealed plates that students do not open, and be autoclaved or bleach-treated before disposal. Never culture bacteria from the human body or from unknown environmental swabs at incubation temperatures near body temperature.

**Dissection ethics.** Dissection should have a clear instructional purpose tied to standards, not be a tradition or spectacle. Specimens should come from legitimate suppliers with humane and legal sourcing, never from roadkill, pets, or student-collected wild animals. Preserved specimens raise a real chemical exposure question: formaldehyde is a known human carcinogen with an OSHA-regulated exposure limit, so prefer specimens preserved in lower-hazard alternatives, ensure good ventilation, and require goggles, gloves, and aprons. Use sharp scalpels correctly, cutting away from the body, on a proper tray, and dispose of blades in a sharps container. Treat animal tissue with respect, brief students beforehand, and provide a meaningful alternative assignment for students who opt out, without penalty or public singling out.

**Lower-hazard substitution.** Substitution is the second-strongest control after elimination, and choosing a safer material is usually better teaching, not a compromise. Common swaps:

| Instead of | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Mercury thermometer | Alcohol or digital thermometer | Mercury is toxic and a spill is a costly hazmat event |
| Concentrated acid or base | Dilute solution, or vinegar and baking soda | Same chemistry concept, far lower burn risk |
| Formaldehyde-preserved specimen | Lower-hazard preservative, model, or virtual dissection | Removes carcinogen exposure |
| Open flame for gentle heating | Hot plate or warm water bath | Removes ignition source near flammables |
| Lead or chromium salts | Nontoxic alternatives | Avoids heavy metal toxicity and disposal cost |
| Bulk chemical quantities | Microscale amounts | Less exposure, less waste, lower cost |

**Trap:** A demonstration is safer than a hands-on lab, so any risky activity can be made acceptable by having the teacher do it in front of the class. Actually a demonstration concentrates the hazard at the front of the room and can put the whole class within range of a splash, spray, or eruption. Hazard is reduced by eliminating or substituting the dangerous material and by proper controls, distance, and shielding, not simply by moving who holds the beaker.

sections.h: Instructional strategy and effective science teaching
sections.body:
Science teaching items reward the answer that puts student thinking and evidence at the center, rather than the answer that maximizes teacher explanation.

**Inquiry along a continuum.** Confirmation and structured inquiry give students the question and procedure; guided inquiry gives the question and lets students design the procedure; open inquiry lets students generate their own questions. Novice classes usually need structure first, moving toward more open inquiry as skills develop. The goal is that students do the sense-making, not that they follow steps to a predetermined result.

**The 5E model** organizes a lesson: **Engage** with a phenomenon or discrepant event that surfaces prior ideas, **Explore** through firsthand investigation before formal terms are introduced, **Explain** by having students articulate patterns and then attaching correct vocabulary, **Elaborate** by applying the idea to a new context, and **Evaluate** throughout. The order matters: experience precedes vocabulary, because a term attached to nothing is memorized and forgotten.

**Addressing misconceptions.** Students arrive with durable prior conceptions that lecture rarely dislodges. Effective practice elicits the idea first, then confronts it with a result the misconception cannot explain, then guides the student to build a better model. Predict, observe, explain routines and discrepant-event demonstrations work because they create the productive surprise.

**Differentiation and access.** Vary complexity, scaffolding, grouping, and product rather than lowering the science content. Support multilingual learners with visuals, hands-on experience, word walls, sentence frames, and cognates rather than simplified science. Provide multiple representations: physical model, diagram, graph, equation, and words. Follow IEP and 504 accommodations, and check that lab stations are physically accessible.

**Assessment.** Formative assessment happens during learning to adjust instruction: exit tickets, whiteboard responses, concept sketches, circulating questions, claim-evidence-reasoning drafts. Summative assessment measures learning at the end. Prefer performance tasks and explanation over recall alone, and use rubrics students see in advance.

**Technology and models.** Simulations, probes, and data tools should extend what hands-on work cannot do: dangerous, invisible, very slow, or very large-scale phenomena. Models are essential to science teaching, and students should build, test, and revise them while recognizing that every model has limits.

**Trap:** The best way to fix a misconception is to state the correct fact clearly and often enough. Actually restating the correct explanation leaves the original mental model intact, and students often hold both and revert under pressure. Change requires the student to confront evidence their existing idea cannot explain and then reconstruct the explanation themselves.

sections.h: Classroom logistics, ethics, and field work
sections.body:
Beyond chemical rules, the science teacher carries management, legal, and ethical duties that show up as scenario questions.

**Supervision and duty of care.** A teacher must provide instruction about the hazard, adequate supervision during the activity, and safe equipment and facilities. Never leave a class unattended during a lab. Students may not work in the lab without supervision or perform unauthorized procedures. Class size and available space genuinely limit which activities are appropriate, and reducing the number of active stations or splitting a rotation is a legitimate safety decision.

**Before any lab.** Do the activity yourself first. Read the SDS for every chemical involved. Give explicit written and verbal safety instructions, including what to do if something goes wrong. Confirm PPE for everyone. Know your evacuation route and where the shutoffs are. Have a plan for students who arrive late or return from absence.

**During and after.** Circulate constantly. Keep aisles and exits clear, keep bags off the floor, and require standing rather than sitting on stools during procedures involving hot or corrosive material. At the end, require cleanup, proper waste segregation, and handwashing. Report every incident, including near misses, in writing according to district policy. Document safety instruction and any signed safety contracts.

**Chemical inventory and waste.** Maintain a current inventory, buy in the smallest workable quantity, date containers on receipt, and remove expired and unknown chemicals through proper hazardous waste channels. Peroxide-forming and shock-sensitive old chemicals are a genuine danger in long-neglected storerooms. Never pour hazardous waste down the drain or put it in the classroom trash.

**Field work.** Obtain permission, scout the site, plan for weather, heat, water, sun, and insects, set a supervision ratio, carry a first aid kit and communication device, know the nearest medical facility, and brief students on site-specific hazards. In Florida that includes heat illness, lightning, water safety, alligators and snakes, fire ants, and venomous plants. Collect responsibly and minimally, follow permit requirements, and leave habitat intact.

**Scientific ethics for students.** Report data honestly, including results that do not fit the hypothesis. Never alter or discard inconvenient data points. Give credit for ideas and sources. Respect living things and human subjects, and get appropriate approval for any study involving people.

**Trap:** Having students sign a safety contract transfers responsibility for accidents to them and their parents. Actually a signed contract documents that instruction occurred and reinforces expectations, but it does not waive the teacher's or district's legal duty of care. The teacher remains responsible for adequate instruction, supervision, and safe conditions.

title: Knowledge of process skills and application of scientific inquiry

sections.h: The nature of science and what science can answer
sections.body:
Science is a way of building explanations of the natural world that must be testable against evidence. Its claims are always open to revision when better evidence appears, which is a strength rather than a weakness.

Features of scientific knowledge: it is based on empirical evidence, it is testable and potentially falsifiable, it is subject to peer review and replication, it is durable but tentative, and it depends on both creativity and logic. Science is also a social enterprise, shaped by collaboration, funding, and the questions a society chooses to ask, while its conclusions are constrained by evidence.

Distinguish **science** from **technology** (applying knowledge to solve practical problems) and from **engineering** (designing solutions under constraints, evaluated by criteria and tradeoffs rather than by a hypothesis test).

**The limits of science.** Science answers questions about the observable natural world that can be tested with evidence. It cannot answer questions of value, morality, meaning, beauty, or the supernatural, because there is no observation that could settle them.

| Testable scientific question | Not answerable by science |
|---|---|
| Does fertilizer concentration affect algal growth rate? | Is it wrong to pollute a river? |
| What is the mercury concentration in this fish? | Should this species be protected at any cost? |
| How does temperature affect coral bleaching? | Which coral reef is the most beautiful? |

Science can tell a community that a nutrient discharge will cause a bloom and estimate the cost of preventing it. Deciding what to do involves values, economics, and politics, which lie outside science even when science informs them.

**Pseudoscience** warning signs: reliance on anecdote and testimonial, claims immune to disproof, appeals to conspiracy to explain lack of evidence, no peer review, and vague terminology.

**Trap:** A scientific idea that has been revised was proved wrong, so science is unreliable. Actually revision in light of new evidence is exactly how science is supposed to work. Well-established ideas are usually refined rather than discarded, and Newtonian mechanics still predicts everyday motion accurately even after relativity extended it.

These four words have precise scientific meanings that differ sharply from everyday usage, and confusing them is one of the most heavily tested points on this exam.

| Term | Definition | Scope | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hypothesis | A testable, falsifiable proposed explanation or prediction for a specific observation | Narrow, one investigation | Plants given fertilizer will grow taller than plants without it |
| Theory | A well-substantiated, broad explanation supported by a large body of evidence from many independent lines of investigation | Broad, explanatory | Plate tectonics, evolution by natural selection, cell theory, atomic theory |
| Law | A statement or equation describing a consistently observed relationship in nature | Descriptive, often mathematical | Newton's law of universal gravitation, law of conservation of mass, Boyle's law |
| Model | A representation of a system used to explain, predict, or communicate | Simplified on purpose | A climate model, a Bohr atom diagram, a food web, a physical DNA model |

The crucial relationships. A theory does not graduate into a law with more evidence; the two do different jobs. A **law describes what happens**, and a **theory explains why**. The law of gravitation lets you calculate the force between two masses; a theory of gravity explains what gravity is. Neither is more certain than the other.

A hypothesis is not simply a guess. It must be testable and must make a prediction that could fail. "Plants like music" is not a hypothesis. "Bean plants exposed to 60 dB of music for 4 hours daily will grow taller over 3 weeks than plants in silence" is, because a result could contradict it. The if-then-because format helps: **if** I add fertilizer, **then** growth will increase, **because** nitrogen limits protein synthesis.

A model is judged by usefulness, not by literal accuracy. Every model omits something. The Bohr atom shows electron energy levels well and electron cloud behavior badly, so a good teacher names the limits.

**Trap:** A theory is just an educated guess, and it becomes a law once scientists prove it. Actually a scientific theory is among the most robust products of science, built from a huge accumulation of evidence, and it never converts into a law. The word "theory" in casual speech means hunch; in science it means the opposite.

A controlled experiment changes one thing on purpose and holds everything else steady, so that any difference in outcome can be attributed to the thing you changed.

| Variable | Definition | Question to ask |
|---|---|---|
| Independent variable | The one factor the researcher deliberately changes | What did I choose to vary? |
| Dependent variable | The outcome measured, which may respond | What am I measuring? |
| Controlled variables (constants) | Everything else deliberately kept the same | What must stay identical? |

The dependent variable **depends on** the independent variable. In a graph, the independent variable goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis, which gives the phrase "DRY MIX": **D**ependent **R**esponding variable on the **Y** axis, **M**anipulated **I**ndependent variable on the **X** axis.

**Worked scenario.** A teacher wants to know whether the amount of fertilizer affects tomato plant growth. She sets up five groups of ten plants each, giving them 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 grams of the same fertilizer per week, and measures plant height in centimeters after six weeks.

- Independent variable: mass of fertilizer per week, in grams.
- Dependent variable: plant height after six weeks, in centimeters.
- Controlled variables: plant variety, pot size, soil type and volume, water amount and schedule, light exposure, temperature, humidity, and starting plant height.
- Control group: the 0 gram group, which receives no fertilizer.
- Sample size: 10 plants per group, which allows averaging to reduce the effect of one unusual plant.

**Control group vs. constant.** These are different things and are frequently confused. The **control group** is the set of subjects that does not receive the treatment, used as a baseline for comparison. A **constant** is a condition held identical across all groups, including the control. In the example above, the 0 gram group is the control group; the identical watering schedule is a constant.

A good design also includes repeated trials, a large enough sample, and where possible blinding or a placebo so expectation cannot shape the result.

**Trap:** An experiment can test several variables at once as long as you measure carefully. Actually if two factors change together you cannot tell which one caused the result: the variables are confounded. Change one independent variable at a time, or use a designed factorial approach that explicitly separates the effects.

The International System of Units gives one agreed unit for each quantity, so measurements are comparable everywhere. Memorize the base units and the prefixes; there is no reference sheet on this test.

| Quantity | SI base unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Length | meter | m |
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Time | second | s |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Amount of substance | mole | mol |
| Electric current | ampere | A |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

Derived units are built from these: volume in m3 or liters, force in newtons (kg*m/s2), energy in joules (N*m), power in watts (J/s), pressure in pascals (N/m2), and density in kg/m3.

Prefixes are powers of ten:

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| giga | G | 10^9 |
| mega | M | 10^6 |
| kilo | k | 10^3 |
| hecto | h | 10^2 |
| deka | da | 10^1 |
| (base) | | 10^0 |
| deci | d | 10^-1 |
| centi | c | 10^-2 |
| milli | m | 10^-3 |
| micro | u (mu) | 10^-6 |
| nano | n | 10^-9 |

Mnemonic for the common ladder: "King Henry Died By Drinking Chocolate Milk" for kilo, hecto, deka, base, deci, centi, milli. Each step is a factor of ten, so moving down the ladder moves the decimal right.

**Worked conversions.** 2.5 km to meters: 2.5 x 1000 = 2500 m. 350 mL to liters: 350 / 1000 = 0.350 L. 4.2 g to milligrams: 4.2 x 1000 = 4200 mg.

**Worked dimensional analysis.** Convert 72 km/h to m/s.

72 km/h x (1000 m / 1 km) x (1 h / 3600 s) = 72,000 / 3600 = 20 m/s.

Useful equivalences: 1 mL = 1 cm3, 1 L of water has a mass of about 1 kg, and 1 metric ton = 1000 kg.

**Trap:** Converting from a small unit to a large unit means multiplying, since the number should get bigger. Actually the number gets smaller when the unit gets larger, because it takes fewer large units to express the same amount. 5000 m is 5 km, not 5,000,000 km. Always check whether your answer is physically sensible.

**Accuracy** is how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value. **Precision** is how close repeated measurements are to each other, and it also refers to the fineness of a measuring instrument. The two are independent: you can have either without the other.

The dartboard picture: darts clustered tightly on the bullseye are accurate and precise; clustered tightly in one corner are precise but not accurate; scattered around the bullseye are roughly accurate on average but not precise; scattered all over are neither.

**Worked example.** A block's true mass is 50.0 g. Three balances each measure it three times.

- Balance A: 50.1, 49.9, 50.0 g. Accurate and precise.
- Balance B: 47.2, 47.3, 47.2 g. Precise but not accurate, which signals a systematic error such as a balance that was never zeroed.
- Balance C: 45.0, 55.0, 50.0 g. Averages to the true value but is not precise, which signals random error.

That distinction matters for troubleshooting. **Systematic error** shifts every measurement the same direction and is fixed by calibrating, zeroing, or correcting the method. **Random error** scatters measurements and is reduced by taking more trials and averaging.

Percent error quantifies accuracy:

```
Percent error = (|measured - accepted| / accepted) * 100
measured = your experimental value (any consistent unit)
accepted = the true or accepted value (same unit)
result is a percentage
```

**Worked example.** A student measures the density of aluminum as 2.60 g/cm3; the accepted value is 2.70 g/cm3.

Percent error = (|2.60 - 2.70| / 2.70) x 100 = (0.10 / 2.70) x 100 = 3.7 percent.

Good practice: read a meniscus at eye level from the bottom of the curve to avoid parallax error, zero the balance before use, estimate one digit beyond the smallest scale marking, and record units every time.

**Trap:** A measurement reported to many decimal places must be accurate. Actually extra digits show only the precision of the instrument or the arithmetic. A poorly calibrated balance can report 47.2385 g for a 50.0 g object, which is precise, detailed, and wrong.

Significant figures communicate how well something was measured, so a calculated result never implies more certainty than the measurements it came from.

Rules for counting significant figures:

1. All nonzero digits count. 47.3 has three.
2. Zeros between nonzero digits count. 2005 has four.
3. Leading zeros never count. 0.0042 has two.
4. Trailing zeros after a decimal point count. 3.200 has four.
5. Trailing zeros with no decimal point are ambiguous. 1500 is usually read as two, and writing 1.500 x 10^3 removes all doubt.
6. Exact counts and definitions are unlimited. 12 students, or 100 cm per meter, do not limit your answer.

Rules for calculating:

- **Multiplication and division:** the answer keeps the fewest number of significant figures among the inputs.
- **Addition and subtraction:** the answer keeps the fewest decimal places among the inputs.

**Worked example (multiplication).** A rectangle measures 4.5 cm by 2.34 cm.

Area = 4.5 x 2.34 = 10.53 cm2. The input 4.5 has two significant figures, so report **11 cm2**.

**Worked example (addition).** 12.11 g + 8.9 g + 1.234 g = 22.244 g. The input 8.9 has one decimal place, so report **22.2 g**.

**Scientific notation** writes a number as a coefficient between 1 and 10 times a power of ten. It handles very large and very small values and makes significant figures unambiguous.

```
N x 10^a
N = coefficient, 1 <= N < 10
a = integer exponent; positive for large numbers, negative for small
```

**Worked conversions.** 93,000,000 becomes 9.3 x 10^7. 0.00052 becomes 5.2 x 10^-4. Reading back, 6.02 x 10^23 is 602 followed by 21 more zeros.

To multiply, multiply coefficients and add exponents: (2.0 x 10^3)(3.0 x 10^4) = 6.0 x 10^7. To divide, divide coefficients and subtract exponents.

**Trap:** A negative exponent means the number itself is negative. Actually a negative exponent means the number is between 0 and 1. 5.2 x 10^-4 equals 0.00052, a small positive number. Only a minus sign in front of the coefficient makes the value negative.

sections.h: Analyzing data: mean, median, mode, and range
sections.body:
Descriptive statistics summarize a data set so a pattern becomes visible. Know how to compute each and, more importantly, when each is the right choice.

```
Mean = (sum of all values) / (number of values)
Median = the middle value when data are ordered; average the two middle values if the count is even
Mode = the value that appears most often; there can be none, one, or several
Range = maximum value - minimum value
Units: all four carry the unit of the original data, except that mode may be a category
```

**Worked example.** Plant heights in cm: 12, 15, 15, 18, 40.

Mean = (12 + 15 + 15 + 18 + 40) / 5 = 100 / 5 = 20 cm.

Median: ordered already, the middle of five values is the third, so 15 cm.

Mode = 15 cm, since it appears twice.

Range = 40 - 12 = 28 cm.

Notice that the mean, 20 cm, is larger than four of the five measurements. The single value of 40 pulled it up. That is exactly why the **median is the better measure of center when the data contain outliers or are skewed**, and why household income is usually reported as a median. The mode is the only usable measure of center for categorical data such as favorite biome or eye color.

**Worked example 2 (even count).** Test scores: 70, 75, 82, 90. Median = (75 + 82) / 2 = 78.5.

Range measures spread but uses only the two extremes, so one outlier can dominate it. Standard deviation gives a fuller measure of spread, describing how far typical values sit from the mean; a small standard deviation means tightly clustered data.

An **outlier** should be investigated, not silently deleted. It may reveal a measurement mistake, a mislabeled sample, or a genuine and interesting result. Report it and explain how you treated it.

**Trap:** The mean is always the best single number to describe a data set. Actually the mean is distorted by outliers and skew. With the heights above, saying the typical plant was 20 cm tall misrepresents a group where four plants were 18 cm or shorter. Choose the median when extreme values are present.

Choosing the right graph is a testable skill, because the graph type follows from the kind of data and the question being asked.

| Graph type | Use it when | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Line graph | Both variables are continuous and you are showing change, usually over time | Temperature each hour for a day |
| Scatter plot | Looking for a relationship or correlation between two continuous measured variables | Fertilizer mass vs. plant height |
| Bar graph | The independent variable is categorical or discrete, comparing amounts across groups | Average height by soil type |
| Histogram | Showing the distribution of one continuous variable in bins | Number of students in each score range |
| Circle (pie) graph | Showing parts of a single whole that sum to 100 percent | Composition of dry air |
